blocks: [F6] [[thm-dolbeault-cohomology-polydisc-vanishes-positive-q]]: on every coordinate polydisc in $\mathbb C^N$ with $N\ge1$, every smooth $\bar\partial$-closed $(0,q)$-form is $\bar\partial$-exact for $1\le q\le N$. This is a statement about the global Dolbeault complex; its identification with sheaf cohomology is established in step 1.3.
associated_steps: 1.3 Let $D\subseteq W$ be a nonempty coordinate polydisc. By [F3], the smooth Dolbeault sequence on $D$ is an exact resolution of $\mathcal O_D$. Its terms are modules over the sheaf of smooth functions, so [F4] makes them acyclic; [F5] therefore identifies $H^q(D,\mathcal O_D)$ with the cohomology of the displayed global Dolbeault complex. By [F6] that global complex has zero cohomology in degrees $1\le q\le N$, and it is zero in degrees $q>N$. Hence $H^q(D,\mathcal O_D)=0$ for every $q>0$. [F3, F4, F5, F6, given]

blocks: [F9] [[thm-dolbeault-cohomology-polydisc-vanishes-positive-q]]: on an arbitrary coordinate polydisc, every smooth $\bar\partial$-closed $(0,q)$-form for $1\le q\le N$ has a global smooth $\bar\partial$ primitive. No centering at $0$ or relative compactness in another fixed polydisc is required.
associated_steps: 1.3 On this arbitrary $D$, [F7] gives the exact smooth Dolbeault sheaf resolution of $\mathcal O_D$. Its terms are modules over smooth real-valued functions; [F8] makes them acyclic and identifies $H^q(D,\mathcal O_D)$ with the cohomology of their global complex. By [F9] that complex has zero cohomology for $1\le q\le N$, and its terms are zero above degree $N$. Hence $H^q(D,\mathcal O_D)=0$ for every $q>0$. [A1, F7, F8, F9, given]

blocks: [F10] Under full AC, positive-degree Dolbeault cohomology of smooth forms vanishes on a product of finite discs and/or $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-dolbeault-cohomology-polydisc-vanishes-positive-q]]).
associated_steps: 1.2 The local Dolbeault lemma [F8], applied coefficientwise in a holomorphic frame on coordinate polydiscs in $U_I$, gives local exactness in every positive degree. In degree zero, a smooth function killed by $\bar\partial$ satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations and is holomorphic by [F9]. By [F7] the operators form a complex, so $0\to\mathcal O\to\mathcal A^{0,0}\xrightarrow{\bar\partial}\cdots\xrightarrow{\bar\partial}\mathcal A^{0,r}\to0$ is an exact sheaf resolution. The whole-polydisc statement [F10] also gives positive-degree exactness on each coordinate polydisc. Each $\mathcal A^{0,j}$ is a module over smooth functions, hence is $\Gamma(U_I,-)$-acyclic by [F11]. The resolution cycles lie in the supplied injective-data domain [F13], and [A1] supplies the DC required by [F12]. Applying [F12] identifies $H^q(U_I,\mathcal O)$ with the cohomology of the global Dolbeault complex on $U_I$. [A1, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, F13, given]

blocks: [F6] [[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-local-coherent-polydisc-acyclicity]]: choose $W$ for the particular coherent module $\mathcal Q_U$ of this example. Then $H^q(D,\mathcal Q_U|_D)=0$ for $q>0$ on every nonempty coordinate polydisc $D\subseteq W$. This choice of $W$ depends on $\mathcal Q_U$.
associated_steps: 3.1 By [F4], $\Gamma(D,i_*\mathbb C)=\mathbb C$, so step 2.1 gives $\Gamma(D,\mathcal Q)\cong\mathbb C$. By step 1.1, $\mathcal Q=\mathcal Q_U|_D$; apply [F6] with the $W$ chosen for $\mathcal Q_U$ to obtain $H^q(D,\mathcal Q)=0$ for every $q>0$. [F1, F2, F4, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

blocks: [A3] Local coherent polydisc acyclicity: “Assume AC. Let $F$ be coherent analytic on a neighborhood of a point $x$ in $\mathbb C^N$. There is a coordinate polydisc $W$ about $x$ such that for every nonempty coordinate polydisc $D\subset W$ and every $q>0$, $H^q(D,F|_D)=0$. Scalar sheaf cohomology on such $D$ is computed by its smooth Dolbeault resolution. One can choose $W$ subordinate to a partial finite-rank free resolution of $F$ of length exceeding $2N$. The assertion is local in the supplied resolution neighborhood; no untwisted projective Cartan A/B or global Stein generation theorem is asserted.” ([[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-local-coherent-polydisc-acyclicity]]). Only its positive-degree polydisc vanishing clause is used below.
associated_steps: 3.1 Let two finite presentations be given near a point $x$, with coherent relation kernels $K,K'$ by [A2]. Apply [A3] to both kernels and intersect the resulting polydisc neighborhoods with the presentation neighborhoods. On a sufficiently small coordinate polydisc $D$ in this intersection, $H^1(D,K)=H^1(D,K')=0$. The long exact sequence [F5] for each presentation then proves that both section maps on $D$ are surjective. More generally, on any common open set $W$ where both presentations are defined and their section maps are surjective, lift the images of the finitely many basis sections of the first free module through the second section surjection. These lifts form a holomorphic matrix $A$ on $W$ with $\pi'A=\pi$. Multiplication by $A$ is continuous for compact-convergence because its entries are bounded on compact subsets; it induces the identity continuously between the quotient topologies. Reversing the presentations gives the reverse continuous identity. Thus the quotient topologies agree on each common presentation neighborhood. A holomorphic change of chart preserves compact-convergence because it and its inverse send compact subsets to compact subsets. [A1, A2, A3, F1, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, given, construct]

blocks: [A2] Local coherent polydisc acyclicity: “Assume AC. Let $F$ be coherent analytic on a neighborhood of a point $x$ in $\mathbb C^N$. There is a coordinate polydisc $W$ about $x$ such that for every nonempty coordinate polydisc $D\subset W$ and every $q>0$, $H^q(D,F|_D)=0$. Scalar sheaf cohomology on such $D$ is computed by its smooth Dolbeault resolution. One can choose $W$ subordinate to a partial finite-rank free resolution of $F$ of length exceeding $2N$. The assertion is local in the supplied resolution neighborhood; no untwisted projective Cartan A/B or global Stein generation theorem is asserted.” ([[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-local-coherent-polydisc-acyclicity]]). Only its positive-degree polydisc vanishing clause is used below.
associated_steps: 1.2 Suppose $1\le r\le3$ and fix $x\in P^r$. Apply [A1] to $\mathcal F$ at $x$ with length $2r$ to obtain a chart neighborhood $W_0$ with a partial free resolution. Its first relation kernel $K_0$ is coherent by [A1]. Apply [A1] again to $K_0$ at $x$ with length $2r$, and choose a neighborhood $W_1\subseteq W_0$ on which that kernel resolution is defined. Apply [A2] to $\mathcal F$ at $x$ to obtain a polydisc neighborhood $W_2$. Choose concentric coordinate polydiscs $D'_x\Subset D_x$ with $\overline{D_x}\subseteq W_1\cap W_2$. Then $D'_x$ is a neighborhood of $x$. [A1, A2, F2, given, construct]

2.1 The sets $D'_x$ cover $P^r$. Compactness [F1] gives finitely many centers $x_1,\ldots,x_s$ whose smaller polydiscs still cover; set $U_i=D_{x_i}$ and $U'_i=D'_{x_i}$. Each singleton $U_i$ and $U'_i$ is $\mathcal F$-acyclic by [A2]. For every nonempty finite intersection of at least two of the $U_i$, the intersection lemma [F4] applies using the length-$2r$ resolution of $\mathcal F$ on the closure of any participating $U_i$. It also applies to the corresponding intersections of the $U'_i$, since their closures lie inside those same resolution neighborhoods. Thus both finite covers are acyclic for $\mathcal F$. [A1, A2, F1, F4, step 1.2]

4.2 To compare two finite admissible covers, retain the given presentation $\pi_I$ on every nonempty intersection $U_I$ of either parent cover, and write $K_I=\ker\pi_I$; there are only finitely many such coherent kernels by [A1]. First shrink each parent cover to open sets $B_i$ with $\overline{B_i}\subset U_i$, still covering $P^r$: at every point choose a coordinate polydisc with compact closure in some parent member, take a finite subcover by compactness [F1], and for each parent member take the union of its finitely many assigned polydiscs. Do this for both parent covers. At a point $x$, repeat step 1.2 for $\mathcal F$ and its new presentation kernel. In addition, for every parent intersection $U_I$ containing $x$, use [A1] to choose a length-$2r$ resolution neighborhood of its particular kernel $K_I$. Intersect these finitely many neighborhoods. Choose nested polydiscs $D'_x\Subset D_x$ whose closures lie in this intersection and in one selected $B_i$ from each parent cover. Also choose $\overline{D_x}$ disjoint from every $\overline{B_j}$ whose parent $U_j$ does not contain $x$; those are finitely many closed sets missing $x$. Compactness gives a finite cover $\mathcal W$ by some of the $D'_x$, with the selected parent assignments. As in steps 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1, its intersections are $\mathcal F$-acyclic and have surjective finite-presentation section maps. Now take a nonempty refined intersection $T=D'_{x_0}\cap\cdots\cap D'_{x_k}$ and one parent cover. Let $I$ be its distinct assigned parent indices. Since $D'_{x_0}$ meets each selected $B_i$, the avoidance condition implies $x_0\in U_i$ for every $i\in I$. Hence the closure of $D'_{x_0}$ lies inside a resolution neighborhood for this very $K_I$. Applying [F4] to $K_I$ on $T$ gives $H^1(T,K_I)=0$, so [F9] proves surjectivity of the section map of the SAME parent presentation $\pi_I|_T$. Its section map on $U_I$ is surjective by parent admissibility. Moreover $\overline T$ is compact in $U_I$, since each refined polydisc has compact closure in its assigned parent. Thus [F5] applies to $\Gamma(U_I,\mathcal F)\to\Gamma(T,\mathcal F)$ using that common presentation. By [F3], the resulting target quotient topology agrees with the chosen one on $T$. This works for both parent covers and all tuples; no newly chosen presentation is substituted for a parent presentation without proving its section surjectivity. [A1, A2, F1, F3, F4, F5, F9, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

blocks: [F11] For $0\le r\le3$, $H^0(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$ and $H^q(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=0$ for every $q>0$ ([[lem-qftx-gaga-projective-cover-laurent-cohomology]]).
associated_steps: 5.1 For $E=\mathcal O_X$, [F10] identifies its holomorphic-section sheaf with $\mathcal O$. Then [F11] supplies $H^0(X,\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$ and $H^q(X,\mathcal O)=0$ for $q>0$ in every stated dimension, as claimed. [F10, F11, given, algebra] ∎

blocks: [F3] Under full AC, on each nonempty standard-cover intersection, sections of $\mathcal O(k)$ have unique normally convergent mixed Laurent–Taylor modes; modes occur exactly for $N(m)\subseteq I$, restrictions preserve the coefficient, every proper nonempty $N(m)$ mode contracts by the stated insertion formula with locally uniform convergence, and the fixed-cover Čech cohomology computes analytic sheaf cohomology ([[lem-qftx-gaga-projective-cover-laurent-cohomology]]).
associated_steps: 2.1 For each nonzero mode choose its least $j\notin N(m)$. On an increasing output index $I$ of size $p$, put $(h_mc)_I=0$ if $j\in I$ and otherwise put $(h_mc)_I=(-1)^{\#\{i\in I:i<j\}}c_{I\cup\{j\}}$. For an input index $I$ of size $p+1$ with $j\notin I$, the term of $h_m\delta c$ deleting $j$ has the same sign as the insertion sign, hence contributes $+c_I$; for every $i\in I$, the term deleting $i$ in $h_m\delta c$ and the term deleting $i$ in $\delta h_mc$ have opposite signs because the order of inserting $j$ and deleting $i$ is reversed. If $j\in I$, then $h_m\delta c$ vanishes and the only nonzero term in $\delta h_mc$ deletes $j$; its two signs agree and give $+c_I$. Terms deleting a vertex of $N(m)$ vanish because the resulting index does not contain $N(m)$. Therefore $\delta h_m+h_m\delta=\mathrm{id}$ in every degree for all six possible $N(m)$. [A1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The modewise formula defines a homotopy on actual holomorphic cochains: by [F3], each output component is a sum of subseries grouped by at most the three choices of $j\notin I$, each retained mode has no negative exponent at the added coordinate, and the subseries converge locally uniformly on $U_I$. Consequently their sums are holomorphic on $U_I$, including across the added coordinate hyperplane, and the coefficient identity in step 2.1 is an identity of analytic cochains. [A1, F3, step 2.1]

4.1 Every nonzero mode is contractible by steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1, while the zero mode has the cohomology computed in step 2.2. The unique normally convergent coefficient expansions and their cochain homotopies make this coefficientwise computation valid for holomorphic sections, and [F3] identifies the resulting fixed-cover Čech cohomology with analytic sheaf cohomology. Hence the displayed sheaf-cohomology values follow. [A1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 2.2, algebra]

blocks: [F4] Under full AC, on the standard cover each section has unique normally convergent degree-$k$ Laurent–Taylor modes; the coefficient occurs on $U_I$ exactly when $N(m)\subseteq I$, restrictions preserve it, every nonempty proper negative set contracts with locally uniform convergence, and the fixed-cover Čech cohomology is analytic sheaf cohomology ([[lem-qftx-gaga-projective-cover-laurent-cohomology]]).
associated_steps: 1.1 A global section restricts to every singleton chart $U_i$. Its coefficient mode $m$ must therefore occur on every $U_i$, so [F4] requires $N(m)\subseteq\{i\}$ for all $i$. Since $r\ge1$, there are at least two distinct singleton charts, whose intersection as index sets is empty; hence $N(m)=\varnothing$ and every $m_i\ge0$. For total degree $-1$, the equation $\sum_i m_i=-1$ is then impossible. Thus the degree-zero Čech cocycles for $\mathcal O(-1)$ are zero, and the fixed-cover comparison in [F4] gives $H^0(X,\mathcal O(-1))=0$. [A1, F1, F3, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 The top Čech cochains have the single index set $J=\{0,\ldots,r\}$. A degree-$k$ mode appears there with no restriction beyond $N(m)\subseteq J$. It is a top coboundary exactly when its negative set is contained in at least one codimension-one face $J\setminus\{j\}$, equivalently when $N(m)\ne J$: one implication follows because the input cochain on that face has no coefficient unless $N(m)\subseteq J\setminus\{j\}$; conversely, if $N(m)\ne J$, choose $j\in J\setminus N(m)$ and the contraction of [F4] supplies a preimage in that face. Therefore top cohomology has exactly the modes with $N(m)=J$. [A1, F4, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 For $k=-r-1$, if every $m_i<0$, write $m_i=-1-n_i$ with integers $n_i\ge0$. The total-degree equation becomes $-(r+1)-\sum_i n_i=-(r+1)$, so $\sum_i n_i=0$ and every $n_i=0$. Thus the only surviving mode is $m=(-1,\ldots,-1)$, and its coefficient space is $\mathbb C$. The normal convergence and analytic cochain contraction in [F4] show that this coefficient quotient is the actual analytic Čech quotient. The comparison in [F4] now gives $H^r(X,\mathcal O(-r-1))\cong\mathbb C$. [A1, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

blocks: [[lem-qftx-gaga-projective-cover-laurent-cohomology]]

[F2] For the standard projective cover and $k=0,-1,-r-1$, the actual analytic twisting sheaves have acyclic intersections; their analytic sheaf cohomology is the normally convergent Laurent–Čech complex. For every integer twist, restrictions preserve Laurent coefficients and the stated mode contractions converge on the output charts. [[lem-qftx-gaga-projective-cover-laurent-cohomology]]
associated_steps: 1.1 A global section of $\mathcal O(-k)$, $k=1,2$, would have an entire coefficient $f_0(t)$ with $f_0(t)=t^{-k}f_\infty(1/t)$. By the normally convergent expansions in [F2], the left side has only powers $t^n$ with $n\ge0$, whereas the right side has only powers $t^n$ with $n\le-k$. Uniqueness of Laurent coefficients forces every coefficient to vanish. Thus both degree-zero groups vanish. [F1, F2, A1, given, algebra]

2.1 A one-cochain on the two-chart overlap has a normally convergent Laurent expansion $g(t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_nt^n$. Coboundaries subtract the entire $t$-series with $n\ge0$ and the series $t^{-k}f_\infty(1/t)$ with $n\le-k$. These two tails converge on their respective entire charts by [F2]; the cover is acyclic for both twists because $r=1$ and $k=1,2$. For $k=1$ they exhaust every integer exponent, so the analytic first cohomology is zero. For $k=2$ the sole remaining exponent is $n=-1$; its coefficient cannot be a coboundary, and it identifies the analytic first cohomology with $\mathbb C$. [F1, F2, A1, step 1.1, algebra]

blocks: [F1] Holomorphic section spaces carry compact-convergence Fréchet topologies, and the coherent section quotients are well-defined Fréchet spaces ([[def-qftx-gaga-frechet-space]], [[lem-qftx-gaga-coherent-section-topology-well-defined]]).
associated_steps: 2.1 Use the compact exhaustion $K_j=\{z\in\Omega':|z|\le j,\ \operatorname{dist}(z,\mathbb C^m\setminus\Omega')\ge1/j\}$, with distance to the empty set taken as $+\infty$. Each $K_j$ is compact by [F6], and their union is $\Omega'$. On each nonempty $K_j$, the family from step 1.1 is equicontinuous and pointwise relatively compact: its values lie in a bounded subset of $\mathbb C^p$, whose closure is compact by [F6] (for $p=0$ the target is the singleton). Apply [F3] and take nested subsequences diagonally; every sequence in the restrictions of $B$ then has a subsequence converging uniformly on every $K_j$. Its limit is holomorphic by [F4]. By [F1] the compact-convergence topology on $\mathcal O(\Omega')^p$ is metrizable, so this sequential compactness proves that the restricted set has compact closure. Thus restriction $\mathcal O(\Omega)^p\to\mathcal O(\Omega')^p$ sends the neighborhood $B$ to a set with compact closure. [A1, F1, F3, F4, F6, step 1.1]

3.1 Let $Q$ and $Q'$ be the quotient maps from the finite free section spaces onto $\Gamma(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ and $\Gamma(\Omega',\mathcal F)$. The image $N=Q(B)$ is a neighborhood of zero because a quotient map is open. Every section in $N$ has a lift in $B$, so the restriction identity $\operatorname{res}_{\mathcal F}\circ Q=Q'\circ\operatorname{res}_{\mathcal O}$ puts $\operatorname{res}_{\mathcal F}(N)$ inside $Q'(\operatorname{res}_{\mathcal O}(B))$. The latter has compact closure, being a continuous image of the compact closure from step 2.1. Thus the coherent-section restriction is compact. [F1, F5, step 2.1, given] ∎

blocks: [A4] On $\mathbb P^r(\mathbb C)$, $0\le r\le3$, coherent analytic cohomology is finite-dimensional in every degree, with the supplier's precise section and quotient topology assertions. [[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-compact-projective-coherent-finiteness]]
associated_steps: 5.2 Fix $q>0$ and a nonzero $s_0$. For $q=1$, the eventual surjections in step 4.2 make the finite dimensions in [A4] nonincreasing integers, hence eventually constant; thereafter multiplication by $s_0$ is an isomorphism. For $q\ge2$ it is already eventually an isomorphism. Choose $N$ beyond this range, put $V=H^q(\mathcal M(N))$, and identify each $H^q(\mathcal M(n))$, $n\ge N$, with $V$ by successive multiplication by $s_0$. A second independent section $s_1$ induces an endomorphism $T_n$ on $V$ between successive degrees. The commuting multiplication square gives $T_{n+1}=T_n=T$. If $V\ne0$, choose an eigenvalue $\lambda$ by [F7]. Multiplication by the nonzero section $s_1-\lambda s_0$ then induces $T-\lambda I$, singular at every such degree. But step 4.2 applied to this fixed section is eventually an isomorphism for $q\ge2$; for $q=1$ it is eventually surjective between spaces of the same stabilized dimension and hence an isomorphism too. This contradiction proves eventual vanishing. The eigenvalue is chosen before its section's threshold; no bound uniform over an infinite pencil is used. [A4, F7, step 4.2, algebra]

blocks: [F1] On compact projective space, every cohomology group of a coherent analytic module is finite-dimensional and Hausdorff in the coherent-section Čech topology ([[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-compact-projective-coherent-finiteness]]). This example determines the exact dimensions for finite support.
associated_steps: 1.1 By [F1], the cohomology groups in the Statement are finite-dimensional under the stated compactness and coherence assumptions. If $S=\varnothing$, [F4] makes $\mathcal F=0$, so all claims hold with $\ell=0$. Suppose $S\ne\varnothing$. Since $S$ is finite and $P^r$ is Hausdorff, choose pairwise disjoint open neighborhoods $V_x$ of its points, one for each $x\in S$ by [F5]. On $V_x\setminus\{x\}$ every stalk of $\mathcal F$ vanishes by the definition of $S$, so the restriction there is the zero sheaf by [F4]. [F1, F4, F5, given, construct]

blocks: [F1] The compact projective coherent-finiteness theorem asserts finite-dimensional Hausdorff cohomology for coherent analytic modules on $P^1$ ([[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-compact-projective-coherent-finiteness]]); the calculation below determines the exact nonzero group.
associated_steps: 3.1 The quotient computation in step 2.1 and the Leray identification in step 1.2 give $H^1(P^1(\mathbb C),\mathcal O(-2))\cong\mathbb C$. In particular, [F1] supplies the compact coherent finiteness conclusion while this calculation exhibits a nonzero positive-degree group. This is a direct analytic Čech calculation using one-variable Laurent series; it invokes neither GAGA nor a positive-twist theorem. [F1, step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎

blocks: [[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-projective-dolbeault-scalar-cohomology]]

[A1] For every finite-rank holomorphic bundle $G$ on $\mathbb P^r(\mathbb C)$, $0\le r\le3$, analytic sheaf cohomology is canonically the global smooth Dolbeault quotient. [[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-projective-dolbeault-scalar-cohomology]]
associated_steps: 3.1 By [A1], a sheaf class has a global smooth closed representative $\alpha$. Its vertical restriction has harmonic part $s(x)\sigma_x$, where $s(x)=\int_{L_x}\iota_x(\alpha_V)$ componentwise in $E_x$. This is smooth by integration over compact fibres. Solve $\gamma_x=B(\alpha_V-s\sigma_x)$; then $\bar\partial_V\gamma_x=\alpha_V-s\sigma_x$. Step 2.1 makes $\gamma$ smooth. A change of unit quaternionic frame acts by an $SU(2)$ fibre isometry and a change of unitary $E$ frame acts by a matrix constant on each fibre; both preserve the equation. Uniqueness from $H^{0,0}(\mathcal O(-2))=0$ makes these local solutions agree. Hence $\gamma$ is global and $\alpha_H:=\alpha-s\sigma-\bar\partial_F\gamma$ annihilates vertical tangent, proving the asserted decomposition. The harmonic/exact orthogonality and the same zero kernel prove its uniqueness. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct]

blocks: [A1] The actual batch-67 carrier states that under full AC, for each $r\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ and every finite-rank holomorphic vector bundle $G$ on $\mathbb P^r(\mathbb C)$, the canonical comparison $H^q(X,\mathcal O(G))\cong H^q_{\bar\partial}(X,G)$ holds for every $q\ge0$; for the trivial line it also states $H^0(X,\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$ and $H^q(X,\mathcal O)=0$ for $q>0$. This matches the comparison used here. This is the local analytic Dolbeault-resolution comparison, whose hypotheses match the present holomorphic-bundle use; it asserts no algebraic-to-analytic GAGA. [[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-projective-dolbeault-scalar-cohomology]]

blocks: [[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-projective-dolbeault-scalar-cohomology]]

[A1] Under full AC, the batch-67 scalar cohomology theorem states that for every $0\le r\le3$, $H^0(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$ and $H^q(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=0$ for $q>0$. [[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-projective-dolbeault-scalar-cohomology]]
[[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-projective-dolbeault-scalar-cohomology]]
associated_steps: 1.1 Fix $r\in\{1,2,3\}$. In the first sequence of [F1], the map $H^0(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)\to H^0(\mathbb P^{r-1},\mathcal O)$ is restriction of constants and hence is the identity $\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$. Exactness therefore gives $H^0(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O(-1))=0$. The adjacent higher groups of $\mathcal O$ and $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{r-1}}$ vanish by [A1]; the long exact sequence then gives $H^q(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O(-1))=0$ for every $q>0$. [given, A1, F1, algebra]

blocks: [[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-projective-dolbeault-scalar-cohomology]]

[A1] Under full AC, the batch-67 scalar cohomology theorem states
$H^0(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$ and
$H^q(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=0$ for $q>0$ for $0\le r\le3$.
[[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-projective-dolbeault-scalar-cohomology]]
associated_steps: 1.1 First the holomorphic monad maps have homogeneous linear entries. Indeed, in the $m=1$ sequence of [F10], $H^1(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=0$ by [A1], so restriction $H^0(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O(1))\to H^0(\mathbb P^{r-1},\mathcal O(1))$ is surjective and its kernel is the defining hyperplane coordinate times $H^0(\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$. Starting with $r=0$, where $\mathcal O(1)$ on a point has one-dimensional section space, induction shows that every section is a linear combination of the homogeneous coordinates: subtract the global coordinate lifts of its restriction, then the remaining section is a constant multiple of the defining coordinate. This applies to entries of both $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal O(-1),\mathcal O)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal O,\mathcal O(1))$. Thus no algebraic/analytic comparison is needed to introduce their four coefficient maps. By [A1] and [F9], the hyperplane sequences and analytic scalar theorem give exactly the negative-twist vanishings required by [F1]. Apply [F1] to the pairing isomorphism; it gives the unique constant Hermitian lift $H$ with the signed identities there. Thus no algebraic cohomology group is being substituted for the analytic lifting groups. [A1, A2, F1, F9, F10, construct]

1.2 For the algebraic $\mathbb P^3_A=\operatorname{Proj}A[\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\mu_1,\mu_2]$ family category, [F11] directly supplies the needed $\mathcal O(-1)$ and $\mathcal O(-2)$ groups over $A$ and $H^0(\mathcal O_A)=A$. Separately, on the analytic first-order thickening each twist has the split underlying analytic sheaf $\mathcal O_A(d)=\mathcal O(d)\oplus\epsilon\mathcal O(d)$; finite direct sums commute with sheaf cohomology, so [F9] gives the same vanishings there. Thus a holomorphic family pairing can be lifted analytically, whereas algebraic family sheaves use [F11]; neither computation substitutes algebraic cohomology for an analytic group or invokes GAGA. Both yield constant $A$-valued chain maps. In both categories the two kernel/image sequences identify global sections with the same constant coefficient kernel of $\beta_A$, so the specified global-section base-change condition is respected by this identification. Repeating the obstruction and ambiguity calculation of [F1] over these coefficient modules lifts the family pairing uniquely to an $A$-linear constant chain isomorphism with Hermitian middle matrix $H_A$; its inverse exists because its reduction is invertible. Global section base change identifies $H^0(F_A)$ with the constant coefficient kernel $L_A$ in $S_A$. Its reduction is injective, so a full-rank minor is a unit and $L_A$ is a direct summand. [A1, A2, F1, F6, F9, F11, construct]

blocks: [F4] Both Dolbeault groups of $\mathcal O(-1)$ vanish. [[lem-qftx-coupled-penrose-fibre-dolbeault]]
associated_steps: 1.1 For the global metric splitting, the mixed component of $\bar\partial(s\sigma)$ is a vertical degree-one form with coefficient $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}\otimes E_x$. On a fibre it has a unique vertical primitive by [F4]. The fixed-fibre $B=\bar\partial^*G$ construction and smooth-parameter difference-quotient argument in [F2], with the estimates [F5], make that primitive smooth over the base. The same fibrewise uniqueness makes it agree across frame and chart changes. Denote the horizontal correction by $\phi(s)$; then $\psi(s)=s\sigma+\phi(s)$ has zero mixed differential. If $s$ is the image of a closed representative $\alpha$, [F2]'s decomposition and closedness say that its horizontal remainder solves this same mixed equation. The difference is fibrewise holomorphic in $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}\otimes E_x$, hence zero by [F4]. Thus $\psi(s)=\alpha-\bar\partial_F\gamma$ is closed for a class image. The differential can still have a horizontal degree-two component for arbitrary $s$; the curvature component of the metric splitting is retained. [A1, F2, F4, F5, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 These local forms are regular on the complete projective fibre. For $w=1/t$, the horizontal vectors are $\widetilde H_i=wH_i$, $\widetilde\theta^i=w^{-1}\theta^i$, and $\widetilde e=w^2e$. Thus the new horizontal coefficients are $\widetilde h_i=t h_i$. They become $c(D_{\bar1}u+\bar wD_2u)/(1+|w|^2)$ and $c(D_{\bar2}u-\bar wD_1u)/(1+|w|^2)$, both smooth. The vertical coefficient changes to $-c u\,d\bar w/(1+|w|^2)^2$ in frame $\widetilde e$, also smooth. The sign is the canonical-coordinate transition, not a change of harmonic normalization. Therefore $\psi_{\mathrm{loc}}$ exists over every entire fibre above this base chart. Its difference from the intrinsic form of step 1.1 has zero vertical part and zero mixed differential. By [F4] that difference is zero. This proves that the coordinate calculation computes the actual global correction, despite using a different horizontal splitting for its displayed coefficients. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

6.1 The local expression equals the intrinsically constructed differential by step 3.1. The same construction and calculation apply in any stereographic chart with the unit round metric. Thus it patches smoothly across the base overlap and infinity; a chartwise solution satisfies the invariant operator equation globally. For the class image $s$, the residual vanishes by step 1.1, and the nonzero frame in step 5.1 gives $(\nabla_A^*\nabla_A+2)s=0$. Gauge changes preserve the fibre normalization and transport the unique mixed correction, while $D_\mu$ and the final operator conjugate by the same unitary frame change. On the dual, $F_{A^\vee}=-F_A^{\mathsf T}$ remains ASD; the identical construction applies. More generally a connection-preserving smooth bundle map commutes with the componentwise vertical projection and inverse, and transports the unique mixed correction; thus the edge and residual construction are natural for such maps, including direct sums. Nothing used irreducibility, absence of parallel sections or nonzero curvature. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

blocks: [[lem-qftx-coupled-penrose-fibre-dolbeault]]

[F1] Each base point has one fibre $L_x\cong\mathbb CP^1$ in the fixed global incidence fibration, and the normalized harmonic generator is intrinsic on that fibre. [[def-qftx-coupled-penrose-incidence-geometry]], [[lem-qftx-coupled-penrose-fibre-dolbeault]]
associated_steps: 1.1 For $x\in U_N\cap U_S$, both chart computations restrict the same global closed form to the same fibre $L_x$. They use the same fibre Dolbeault operator and normalized harmonic projection, so both give the same value $s(x)$. If the global representative changes by $\bar\partial_F\beta$, its vertical restriction changes by $\bar\partial_V\beta$; harmonic forms are orthogonal to exact forms, so the harmonic projection is unchanged. Hence the chart sections agree and are independent of the representative, and they glue to a global section on $S^4$. [F1, F2, algebra]

blocks: [F3] For a compact oriented manifold without boundary, the integral of an exact top form is zero. [[thm-general-stokes-theorem]]
associated_steps: 1.1 The normalized area form is $\omega=(x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy)/(4\pi)$. In spherical coordinates it is $\sin\vartheta\,d\vartheta\wedge d\varphi/(4\pi)$, so its integral over $S^2$ is $1$. It is rotation-invariant. By [F3], it cannot be exact; [F2] then makes $[\omega]$ a generator of $H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(S^2)$. Constants generate $H^0$ and are fixed by $T$, while $H^1=0$. Thus the action on both nonzero cohomology groups is trivial and [F1] gives $\chi_{\operatorname{Ind}_T(E^\bullet)}(g)=1+1=2$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

blocks: [F4] Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If $X$ is an oriented smooth four-manifold with boundary and $\eta$ is a compactly supported smooth three-form, then $\int_Xd\eta=\int_{\partial X}\eta$; an empty boundary contributes zero. [[thm-general-stokes-theorem]]
associated_steps: 2.2 Let $a$ be any smooth adjoint-bundle-valued one-form on compact $S^4$ and vary $A_t=A+ta$. Expanding $F_{A_t}=dA_t+\tfrac12[A_t\wedge A_t]$ gives $F_{A_t}=F_A+t(da+[A\wedge a])+\tfrac12t^2[a\wedge a]$, because the bracket of two one-forms is symmetric under exchange. Symmetry of $\kappa$ and the two-form Hodge inner product then give $\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0S_E[A_t]=g_{\mathrm{YM}}^{-2}\int_{S^4}\kappa((da+[A\wedge a])\wedge *F_A)$. The graded product rule gives $d\kappa(a\wedge *F_A)=\kappa(da\wedge *F_A)-\kappa(a\wedge d*F_A)$. Infinitesimal Ad-invariance, $\kappa([X,Y],Z)=\kappa(X,[Y,Z])$, gives $\kappa([A\wedge a]\wedge *F_A)=\kappa(a\wedge[A\wedge *F_A])$ after the degree-one wedge reorder; adding the identities yields $d\kappa(a\wedge *F_A)=\kappa((da+[A\wedge a])\wedge *F_A)-\kappa(a\wedge D_A*F_A)$. The scalar three-form $\kappa(a\wedge *F_A)$ is globally defined since $\kappa$ is Ad-invariant, and is compactly supported because $S^4$ is compact. By [F4] its exterior derivative integrates to zero on the closed manifold; using step 1.2, the first variation is $g_{\mathrm{YM}}^{-2}\int_{S^4}\kappa(a\wedge D_A*F_A)=0$. This holds for every such $a$, proving the saddle condition in [A1]. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

blocks: [F11] Stokes converts compact disk derivative integrals to their oriented boundary integrals. [[thm-general-stokes-theorem]]
associated_steps: 2.1 For either charged field $f=q,p$, expand $|(D_1+iD_2)f|^2=|Df|^2-B|f|^2+i\{\partial_1(\bar fD_2f)-\partial_2(\bar fD_1f)\}$. Expanding $[B-g^2(\xi-s)]^2/(2g^2)$ gives $B^2/(2g^2)+g^2(\xi-s)^2/2+Bs-\xi B$. Step 1.1 shows all the required nonnegative densities are integrable. If $G(R)=\int_{|x|=R}(|Dq|^2+|Dp|^2)ds$, then [F9] and finite energy give $\int G(R)dR<\infty$. Hence there are increasing radii $R_j\to\infty$ with $R_jG(R_j)\to0$, since an eventual positive lower bound on $RG(R)$ would force logarithmic divergence. Uniform vacuum amplitudes and [F8] bound the boundary-current integral by $C\sqrt{R_jG(R_j)}\to0$. Integrating the two algebraic identities on those disks, using [F11], limiting flux $2\pi n$ and [F10] gives the stated whole-plane identity. For negative n, conjugation reverses flux and changes $D_1+iD_2$ to $D_1-iD_2$ without changing energy. [A1, F1, F2, F8, F9, F10, F11, step 1.1, algebra]

blocks: [F2] Smooth compactly supported forms satisfy Stokes on an oriented manifold with boundary, under its countable-choice scope; on a compact disk this gives the ordinary boundary integral for the one-form $A$. [[thm-general-stokes-theorem]]
associated_steps: 2.1 Use the unitary real-linear change $q=(M+e^{i\beta}\overline{\widetilde M})/\sqrt2$, $p=(M-e^{i\beta}\overline{\widetilde M})/\sqrt2$; both fields have charge +1 and $s=|q|^2+|p|^2$. Their summed covariant-gradient norms equal the original charged norms. Let $E_0$ be the critical two-charge functional with terms $b_0B^2/2+|Dq|^2+|Dp|^2+(s-\xi)^2/(2b_0)$ and no additional p-mass term. The Maxwell bound $b\ge b_-$, step 1.1 and the definition of $\gamma$ give $E_b\ge\gamma E_0$, after dropping the nonnegative neutral gradient. In particular $E_0$ is finite. Uniform vacuum approach makes q,p bounded near infinity, with $|q|\to\sqrt\xi$ and $p\to0$ in the vacuum phase frame. Stokes on disks and the original angular condition give limiting flux $2\pi n$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Write $G(R)=\int_{|x|=R}(|Dq|^2+|Dp|^2)\,ds$. Finiteness of the gradient integral implies $\int_{R_0}^{\infty}G(R)\,dR<\infty$. There are radii $R_j\to\infty$ with $R_jG(R_j)\to0$: otherwise $G(R)\ge\epsilon/R$ eventually for some $\epsilon>0$, contradicting that integral. By [F3] and bounded tail amplitudes, the absolute boundary-current integral $\oint(\bar qDq+\bar pDp)$ on these circles is at most $C\sqrt{R_jG(R_j)}\to0$. For $n>0$, expand the disk square identity using $[D_1,D_2]f=-iBf$ for $f=q,p$: $|(D_1+iD_2)f|^2=|Df|^2-B|f|^2+i\{\partial_1(\bar fD_2f)-\partial_2(\bar fD_1f)\}$ and $b_0[B-b_0^{-1}(\xi-s)]^2/2=b_0B^2/2+(s-\xi)^2/(2b_0)+Bs-\xi B$. Add the identities, integrate, and let $R_j\to\infty$. The boundary current vanishes along this subsequence, the flux tends to $2\pi n$ and the remaining squares are nonnegative, so $E_0\ge2\pi\xi n$. Reflection of the second transverse coordinate proves $E_0\ge2\pi\xi|n|$ for negative n. Step 2.1 now proves the claimed positive bound for every full-model profile. No full-circle boundary-current limit was assumed or inferred from finite energy. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

blocks: [[thm-general-stokes-theorem]]
[F4] [[thm-general-stokes-theorem]] makes an exact top-form integral vanish on the closed sphere.
associated_steps: 4.1 If $T(f,\omega)=0$ with $(f,\omega)\in H^1$, step 3.1 and weak regularity [F3] make both entries smooth and harmonic. By [F2], $f$ is constant and the harmonic two-form is zero, giving a one-dimensional complex kernel. The same vanishing has an elementary check: $d^*\omega=0$ and $*\omega=\omega$ imply $d\omega=0$; since $H^2=0$, write $\omega=d\beta$, and [F4] gives $\|\omega\|_2^2=\int\omega\wedge\overline\omega=\int d(\beta\wedge\overline\omega)=0$. For $T^*\alpha=0$, one has $d^*\alpha=0$ and $d\alpha$ anti-self-dual; hence $\|d\alpha\|_2^2=-\int d\alpha\wedge d\overline\alpha=0$ by [F4]. Thus $\alpha$ is harmonic and is zero by $H^1=0$. The Green inverse $G_1:L^2\to H^2$ of $\Delta_1$, which exists without a kernel by [F2]–[F3], gives the bounded right inverse $T^*G_1:L^2\to H^1$ of $T$. The range is therefore all $L^2$, the kernel is finite, and $T$ is Fredholm with index $1$. The unitary maps in step 2.1 transfer this conclusion to $D^+_{A_+}$. [given, A1, F2, F3, F4, step 3.1, algebra]

blocks: [F6] Stokes applies on the compact oriented four-sphere under countable choice. [[thm-general-stokes-theorem]], [[def-countable-choice]]
associated_steps: 3.1 Let $P\to S^4$ be any smooth principal $U(1)$ bundle. Smooth local connection forms glue by a smooth partition of unity [F5]. Parallel transport from the center of each closed hemisphere along radial segments gives a smooth trivialization: each transported frame solves a linear smooth ODE, and [F5] supplies its smooth dependence on the endpoint. Their transition is a map $g:S^3\to U(1)$. Pulling back the universal cover $\mathbb R\to U(1)$ gives a covering of $S^3$; its connected component through a chosen point is a connected cover, hence is one-sheeted by [F4]. Thus $g$ lifts to $\theta:S^3\to\mathbb R$. Since the covering is a local diffeomorphism and $g$ is smooth, the lift is smooth. The homotopy $\theta_s=(1-s)\theta+s\theta(x_0)$ makes $g$ null-homotopic. Reparameterize this homotopy to be constant near its final parameter and use it on a collar of one hemisphere; this changes that trivialization so the transition is constant and the local frames glue to a global frame. Hence $P$ is trivial. In that frame write the real connection form as $a$ and its curvature as $f=da$, so $df=0$. Then $f\wedge f=d(a\wedge f)$, and Stokes [F6] gives $\int_{S^4}f\wedge f=0$. If it is ASD, $f=-*f$, so $f\wedge f=-f\wedge *f=-|f|^2d\mathrm{vol}$. The zero integral forces $f=0$, and the charge in the Statement is zero. Thus no smooth charge-one $U(1)$ ASD connection exists, and that empty ordinary sector cannot equal the positive-FI quotient $\mathbb C^2$. [F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

blocks: [[thm-general-stokes-theorem]]

[F4] $H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(S^4)=H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(S^4)=0$ and the integral of an exact four-form over the compact boundaryless sphere is zero. [[thm-de-rham-cohomology-of-spheres]], [[thm-general-stokes-theorem]]
associated_steps: 3.1 The coefficientwise ASD equation in this global frame is $(da)^+=0$. Write $a=i\alpha$ for a real one-form. Since $d\alpha$ is ASD, $\int|d\alpha|^2=-\int d\alpha\wedge d\alpha=-\int d(\alpha\wedge d\alpha)=0$ by [F4]. Continuity and nonnegativity imply $d\alpha=0$. Again [F4] gives $\alpha=df$; subtract the constant $f(\infty)$ and put $\phi=-if$. The based gauge $1+\varepsilon\phi$ removes $a$. This gauge is unique: a residual imaginary scalar with zero derivative is constant and its value at infinity is zero. Ordinary framed stabilizers were already trivial in step 1.2. The first-order connection groupoid is therefore the trivial point, not merely a set with one known reduced point. [F4, step 2.1, algebra]

blocks: [F14] Smooth forms on compact annuli satisfy Stokes, giving integration by parts for the logarithmic distribution calculation. [[thm-general-stokes-theorem]]
associated_steps: 1.1 First, $\log|z|^2$ is locally integrable and harmonic off zero. For a smooth compactly supported test function $\varphi$, apply [F14] on an annulus excluding $|z|\le\varepsilon$ to the one-form $\log|z|^2*d\varphi-\varphi*d\log|z|^2$. Its inner-boundary contribution is $-\varepsilon\log(\varepsilon^2)\int_0^{2\pi}\partial_r\varphi(\varepsilon,\theta)d\theta+2\int_0^{2\pi}\varphi(\varepsilon,\theta)d\theta$, which tends to $4\pi\varphi(0)$; the outer contribution is zero. Thus $\Delta\log|z-z_j|^2=4\pi\delta_{z_j}$ by translation. For $z\ne z_j$, put $t_j=a/(|z-z_j|^2+a)$. Then $0<t_j<1$, $e^{u_-}=\prod_j(1-t_j)^{m_j}$, and direct radial differentiation gives $\Delta u_-=-\frac4a\sum_jm_jt_j^2+4\pi\sum_jm_j\delta_{z_j}$ distributionally. If $N>0$, let $t_*:=\max_jt_j$; then $1-e^{u_-}\ge t_*$ and $\sum_jm_jt_j^2\le Nt_*$. Hence $\Delta u_-+\kappa(1-e^{u_-})-4\pi D\ge(\kappa-4N/a)t_*\ge0$. For $N=0$, $u_-=0$ and the subsolution inequality is equality. [given, F1, F14, algebra]

blocks: [F3] [[thm-general-stokes-theorem]]: on the oriented disk with outward-normal-first boundary orientation, the integral of $dA$ equals the boundary integral of $A$, and the integral of $dj$ equals the boundary integral of the one-form $j$.
associated_steps:
2.1 For sufficiently large $r$, $|q|\ge\sqrt\xi/2$. On $\partial D_r$, $j=|q|^2(d(n\theta+\phi)-A)$, so $\int_{\partial D_r}A=2\pi n-\int_{\partial D_r}j/|q|^2$ because $\phi$ is single-valued and periodic. Along the sequence from step 1.2,
$$\left|\int_{\partial D_{r_m}}\frac{j}{|q|^2}\right|\le\frac{2}{\sqrt\xi}(2\pi r_mK(r_m))^{1/2}\longrightarrow0.$$
By [F3], $\int_{D_{r_m}}B\to2\pi n$. [F1, F3, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Integrate the positive-winding disk identity from step 1.1 over $D_{r_m}$ and use [F3] on the current term. The two square integrals are nonnegative, while the boundary-current integral tends to zero by step 1.2 and the flux integral tends to $2\pi n$ by step 2.1. By [F5], the integrals of the nonnegative energy and square densities over the increasing disks converge to their plane integrals, so taking the limit gives the positive-sign exact identity and hence $E(A,q)\ge2\pi\xi n$ for $n\ge0$. For $n\le0$, apply the positive-sign identity from step 1.1 to $(\overline q,-A)$, whose winding is $-n\ge0$; its energy is unchanged and its curvature changes sign. The resulting identity is exactly the negative-sign identity for $(A,q)$ and gives $E(A,q)\ge-2\pi\xi n$. Thus the bound is $E(A,q)\ge2\pi\xi|n|$, and both identities hold when $n=0$ as well. [F3, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

5.1 Let $(a,\eta)$ be a smooth compactly supported variation of a minimizing pair, and set $A_t=A+ta$, $q_t=q+t\eta$; for any field expression $F$, define $\delta F:=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}F(A_t,q_t)$. For sufficiently small $t$, the fields remain in the same boundary sector; outside the compact support they equal the original fields. Thus the boundary-current limit in the disk identity is unchanged and the flux is unchanged by Stokes applied to $d a$. The energy along this variation is the constant $2\pi\xi|n|$ plus the squared $L^2$ norms of the two first-order residuals in step 1.1. Both residuals vanish at $t=0$; differentiating the squared norms gives $E'(0)=0$ and
$$E''(0)=2\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(|\delta(D_{A,1}\pm iD_{A,2})q|^2+\frac{|\delta(B\mp e^2(\xi-|q|^2))|^2}{2e^2}\right)dx_1dx_2\ge0,$$
with the upper signs for $n\ge0$ and lower signs for $n\le0$ (either choice when $n=0$). Therefore the first variation vanishes and no smooth compactly supported same-sector perturbation lowers the energy. Distinct divisors give distinct possible minimizing fields, so no cross-divisor uniqueness follows. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

blocks: [F5] [[thm-general-stokes-theorem]]: the integral of $d\mathcal A$ over a smooth oriented disk or side cylinder equals the oriented boundary integral of $\mathcal A$.
associated_steps: 1.2 For finite $R$, apply [F5] to $D_R\times\{z\}$ to identify its magnetic flux with $\int_{\partial D_R}A_\perp(\cdot,z)$. Apply [F5] to the side $\partial D_R\times[0,L]$: its flux is the difference of the two oriented end-circle integrals. The uniform angular one-form condition makes both integrals $2\pi n+o(1)$, so the side flux tends to zero. Thus the stated angular condition enforces the required no-leakage condition and is consistent with the fixed slice flux. [F5, given, algebra]

[F1] Conditional GAGA on projective spaces: analytification is exact, preserves cohomology and Ext, and commutes with restriction to $L_\infty$; its use here is limited to algebraic-family fiber comparison under the base-change hypotheses in the Statement. [[thm-qftx-projective-gaga-for-monad-data]]
associated_steps: 7.1 For a finite-type algebraic base $S$, tensor the relative diagonal Koszul resolution by the flat family and use the assumed base-change isomorphisms [A1]. The direct-image terms are vector bundles of ranks $k,2k+N,k$, and the finite filtered complex commutes with residue-field restriction. On every fiber, step 6.1 gives the monad. The right end map is surjective on every fiber, hence surjective by Nakayama [F8], and its kernel $K$ is locally free. Locally on $S$, write the remaining exact sequence as $0\to P^{-1}\to K\to\mathcal E\to0$, with $P^{-1}$ and $K$ flat over the base. Tensoring by any residue field $k(s)$ stays injective at the left because the fiber complex is a monad on the whole projective plane. Thus $\operatorname{Tor}_1^{\mathcal O_{S,s}}(k(s),\mathcal E)=0$, equivalently the maximal-ideal multiplication map is injective. Since $\mathcal E$ is finite over the local ring of $\mathbb P^2\times S$, [F6] proves flatness over $S$. The same base-change maps identify the relative middle cohomology with the given family. This is precisely the family range stated and does not assert base change outside it. [A1, F1, F3, F6, F8, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

blocks: [[thm-qftx-projective-gaga-for-monad-data]]
[A1] Absolute projective GAGA on P³ supplies an exact tensor equivalence and cohomology comparison. [[thm-qftx-projective-gaga-for-monad-data]]
associated_steps: 1.1 Algebraize the holomorphic bundle using [A1]. Its algebraic sheaf is locally free: the holomorphic bundle is dualizable, the exact tensor equivalence transports its evaluation and coevaluation and reflects their triangle identities, and those identities give a finite dual basis on each local algebraic chart, hence a finite projective module. In a splitting C⁴=A⊕B into two-planes, a graph chart of G consists of X:A→B and the incidence is (X,[λ])↦[λ,Xλ], with p a product with P(A). In the library quotient convention it is the projective bundle of the dual of the tautological subbundle. Thus [F1] gives properness, finite presentation and flatness, and e*E is a coherent locally free sheaf flat over G. [A1, F1, construct]

2.1 At a real line L, absolute P³ GAGA applied to the coherent algebraic sheaf i*(E|L), for the closed immersion i:L→P³, identifies its cohomology with that of the trivial analytic restriction. This uses no GAGA on the Grassmannian: closed-immersion direct image is exact, and its analytification is the same local quotient-module tensor construction. Hence the algebraic fiber cohomology is C^N in degree zero and zero above by [F3]. Its degree-one base-change map has zero target, so is surjective. By [F2] that map is an isomorphism; the finite stalk of R¹p*e*E has zero residue fiber, and Nakayama kills it on a neighborhood. The degree-one local-freeness criterion of cohomology/base change now gives surjectivity in degree zero. Its degree-zero case makes H=p*e*E a finite locally free rank-N bundle with all degree-zero base-change maps isomorphisms near L. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

4.1 Analytify this actual evaluation isomorphism. On every local product V×P¹, a holomorphic function is constant on each P¹ fiber by the maximum principle, and its remaining function on V is holomorphic by evaluation at a fixed point. Thus p_an*O=O. Trivializing H locally gives p_an*p_an*H_an=H_an, where the inner star denotes pullback and the outer star denotes direct image. Consequently the analytic direct image of e_an*E is H_an, its evaluation is the analytified evaluation, and all degree-zero analytic fiber maps are isomorphisms. The same product calculation after any base change identifies the base-change maps. No circular assumption of analytic base-change surjectivity or broad Grauert theorem is used. [A1, F3, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The quaternionic involution on G sends a graph X to j_B X j_A^{-1}; its fixed graph matrices form the real four-dimensional quaternionic subspace, whose complexification is the entire graph space. These charts embed HP¹ smoothly and totally really into G. On its incidence family evaluation is a diffeomorphism onto Z: the inverse sends [v] to (span_C(v,jv),[v]), smoothly in projective charts, and j²=-1 excludes dependence of v,jv. Restrict H_an to this real locus to obtain the smooth rank-N bundle with the claimed fibers and evaluation. The positive pairing induces its Hermitian matrix by evaluating local section frames at a smoothly chosen point on each line; this proves smoothness and positivity, independently of parallelness. At infinity the given unitary frame induces the section-bundle frame. All arguments use only the stated local absolute comparison. [A1, F4, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

blocks: [[thm-qftx-projective-gaga-for-monad-data]]

[A1] Absolute projective GAGA supplies the exact coherent tensor equivalence and cohomology comparison. The relative-family comparison map is constructed in its current proof and is not a separate assumed theorem. [[thm-qftx-projective-gaga-for-monad-data]]
associated_steps: 2.1 For any Ward bundle use [F3] to form the analytic vector bundle H over a complex-open neighborhood U of every real line in G=Gr(2,4), with holomorphic evaluation p*H≅e*E on the universal family. On a graph chart X:A→B, incidence is (X,[λ])↦[λ,Xλ]. The distribution D=ker(de) consists of matrix variations v with vλ=0 and no λ variation. It is a holomorphic involutive rank-two subbundle, since it is tangent to the fibers of the submersion e. The restriction of p*Ω¹_U to D has kernel B*⊗O(-1) on each projective-line fiber and target D*≅O(1)². The O(-1) vanishings in [F3] give Ω¹_U≅p_*D*. Equivalently, on the graph chart a linear covector on Hom(A,B) restricts to a section on all kernels vλ=0; the map is injective because those kernels span Hom(A,B), and both coefficient spaces have dimension four. This gives the holomorphic sheaf isomorphism without any extra analytic base-change assumption. [A1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

7.1 The explicit incidence chart fixes vertical complex orientation followed by the positive base orientation to be the complex orientation of Z. The pullback of the positive point Thom class on S⁴ is the positive normal Thom class of its fiber CP¹; [F5] identifies its absolute class as the Poincaré dual of that fiber. A linear CP¹ has dual H²: H restricts with integral one to the line, and the integral projective cohomology ring gives H² as its positive degree-four generator. The two suppliers therefore cover the ordinary dictionary for every $N\ge1$ under exactly those inherited hypotheses. Neither identifies the positive-FI resolution or its rank-one formal coefficients with ordinary ASD moduli. [[thm-qftx-zero-fi-regular-adhm-asd-correspondence]], [[lem-qftx-rank-one-regular-adhm-and-ordinary-asd-boundary]]
associated_steps: 2.2 For $N\ge2$, the source and target of [A2]'s rank-two-and-higher supplier agree with the zero-FI regular quotient and the framed ASD sector in the conditional dictionary, with $q_N=-k$ and identical framing and orientation. For $N=1$, stabilize by adding one unused framed line as in the boundary lemma: its moment equations, word stability and costability are unchanged. Its proved boundary identifies the two empty spaces at $k>0$ and the unique framed flat points at $k=0$, and its direct first-order gauge argument supplies the corresponding family identification rather than inferring it from an orbit-set bijection. Thus the ordinary dictionary has no uncovered rank-one case; its exact rank-two analytic and normal-form hypotheses remain inherited. This does not place any positive-FI partition fixed point in the open regular ordinary locus. In particular, the positive-FI one-box rank-one contribution is still the formal coefficient of step 1.1 and is not an ordinary positive-charge abelian instanton. [given, A2, L2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $k>0$, use the tuple $Y_1=\{(i,0):0\leq i<k\}$ and $Y_\alpha=\varnothing$ for $\alpha>1$; step 1.1 constructs a stable datum. Replacing $B_1$ by $B_1+c\,\mathrm{id}_V$ preserves the complex equation and stability while changing $\operatorname{tr}(B_1)$ by $kc$ for every $c\in\mathbb C$. Trace is invariant under conjugation, so the descended trace function on the geometric quotient has image $\mathbb C$, which is not compact. Thus the quotient is noncompact. The completed Borel carrier matches the compact real-Borel interface in [L1]. The ADHM/monad comparisons in [A1]–[A2] retain their exact analytic and family hypotheses, while step 2.3 has supplied the precise intrinsic localized Borel–Moore pushforward covered by [F6]. [given, F1, L1, L2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

blocks: [F2] [[lem-qftx-taubes-disk-barriers-and-monotone-iteration]]: for every exhausting disk $D_R$, it supplies $u_R$ with $u_-\le u_R\le0$, the exact divisor equation and smooth center subtraction, plus $R$-uniform local $W^{2,p}$ and $C^{2,\alpha}$ bounds after subtracting the fixed logarithmic singular function $s$.
associated_steps: 1.1 Choose radii $R_k\to\infty$ with every center in $D_{R_k}$. Let $s=2\sum_jm_j\log|z-z_j|$ and $w_k=u_{R_k}-s$. For each compact disk $K$ and each $0<\alpha<1$, [F2] gives a uniform $C^{2,\alpha}$ bound on $w_k$ on a slightly larger disk. Thus $(w_k,Dw_k,D^2w_k)$ is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous there. Apply the Euclidean sequence statement [F6] to the finite derivative tuple on each nonempty compact disk. A countable diagonal selection under [A1] then gives locally uniform convergence of $w_k$ and all its derivatives through order two. The fundamental theorem of calculus on coordinate segments identifies the limiting derivative tuple as the first and second derivatives of one $C^2$ function w. Thus the subsequence converges in $C^2$ on every compact disk. Set $h=s+w$. [A1, F2, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 On every compact set, $e^{u_{R_k}}=e^s e^{w_k}$ converges uniformly to $e^h$. Passing to the limit in the weak divisor equation for $u_{R_k}$ gives $\Delta h+\kappa(1-e^h)=4\pi D$ distributionally. Since $s-2m_j\log|z-z_j|$ is smooth near each center and $w$ is $C^2$ there, the prescribed logarithmic subtraction extends continuously. The equation for $w$ is $\Delta w=\kappa(e^s e^w-1)$ with smooth coefficient $e^s=|P|^2$; repeated interior Schauder regularity [F4] bootstraps $w$ to $C^\infty$, so each center subtraction is smooth. The bounds $u_-\le u_{R_k}\le0$ pass to the limit, and $u_-(z)\to0$ at infinity; hence $h\le0$ and $h\to0$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

blocks: [F3] [[thm-qftx-critical-vortex-global-energy-minimum]]: a reconstructed fixed-divisor solution attains the absolute transverse minimum $2\pi\xi|n|$ in its winding sector.
associated_steps: 1.2 Apply [F2] to the explicit effective divisor $|n|[0]$ of degree $|n|$ (the empty divisor if $n=0$) and conjugate when $n<0$. Its signed flux is $2\pi n$, and [F3] gives $T_n=2\pi\xi|n|$. [F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Here $P=(z-z_0)^2(z-z_1)$ and $s=2\log|P|$. The reconstruction in [F2] extends smoothly over both centers, solves the positive critical equations, and has flux $2\pi N=6\pi$. Since it is a fixed-divisor reconstructed solution, [F3] gives its attained absolute transverse energy $2\pi\xi N=6\pi\xi$. The argument determines the profile by the unique scalar boundary-value problem and supplies no elementary closed form. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

blocks: [[def-qftx-smooth-sobolev-gauge-configuration|Configuration-space, gauge-action, and topology conventions]]

[F2] The configuration definition sets $\mathcal A_\infty=A_0+\Omega^1(S^r;\operatorname{ad}P)$ with the $C^\infty$ section topology from finite-atlas derivative seminorms, defines $\mathcal G_\infty=\Gamma^\infty(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ with the same section topology, and fixes the local right action $A^u=u^{-1}Au+u^{-1}du$, the based holonomy irreducibility condition, and the quotient topologies. [[def-qftx-smooth-sobolev-gauge-configuration]]
associated_steps: 1.1 Apply [F1] to the specified compact smooth principal bundle $P\to S^r$ to obtain a smooth principal connection $A_0$; fix it as the affine reference used in $\mathcal A^\infty(P)$ and the Sobolev intermediary. This applies to every bundle sector because [F1] uses only local bundle charts and a subordinate partition, not a global trivialization. The based frame and standard metric are already fixed in the Statement. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 Choose the fixed integer $k>r/2+1$. The smooth clause of [F3], applied with the configuration data [F2], makes $q_*$ a locally trivial principal $\overline{\mathcal G}^\infty(P)$-bundle. By [F4], its total space is nonempty, path connected, and has $\pi_j=0$ for every $j\ge1$, so it is weakly contractible in the sense used in [F6]. For a constant central gauge section $u=\zeta I_N$, the local action formula gives $A^u=A$ because $u^{-1}Au=A$ and $du=0$; hence reduced and full gauge groups have the same orbits on $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$. [F2, F3, F4, F6, step 1.1]

4.1 The locus $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$ is gauge invariant: in the chosen frame, the based holonomy subgroup of $A^u$ is $u(p_m)^{-1}\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)u(p_m)$, so it has the same invariant subspaces up to conjugation. It is open: by [F2], the inclusion $\mathcal A^\infty(P)\hookrightarrow\mathcal A_k(P)$ is continuous, as each fixed $H^k$ norm is bounded by finitely many smooth derivative seminorms on the finite compact atlas. The smooth irreducible locus is the inverse image of the Sobolev irreducible locus, which is open by [F3]. The full orbit projection $q$ is open because, for any open $U\subseteq\mathcal A^\infty(P)$, its saturation $q^{-1}(q(U))=\bigcup_{u\in\mathcal G^\infty(P)}U\cdot u$ is open. For fixed smooth $u$, the map $A\mapsto u^{-1}Au+u^{-1}du$ is continuous in every finite-atlas derivative seminorm by the Leibniz rule; its inverse is the same formula for $u^{-1}$, so each gauge translate is a homeomorphism. Therefore $q(\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P))$ is open and $q|_{\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)}$ is an open quotient map onto this subset. The reduced and full actions have the same orbits there, so their quotient topologies identify the reduced orbit space homeomorphically with $q(\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P))$; this proves the claim about $\iota$ in the Statement. If $q$ had a continuous section, its restriction to this open subset would take each irreducible orbit to a point in that same orbit, hence into $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$. Via the stated homeomorphism, this would give a continuous section of $q_*$, contradicting step 3.1. Thus $q$ has no continuous section. [F2, F3, step 3.1, given, construct] ∎

blocks: [F1] The configuration definition fixes the finite-atlas norms, $\operatorname{ad}P$, the right-action formula, and the covariant derivative $d_A\xi=d\xi+[A,\xi]$. [[def-qftx-smooth-sobolev-gauge-configuration]]
associated_steps: 1.1 On an overlap of two relatively compact bundle charts, a localized section changes coordinates by multiplication by a smooth transition matrix and by a smooth coordinate change. Every derivative of order at most $k$ of the transformed coefficient is a finite sum of bounded derivatives of these transition maps times derivatives of the original coefficient of order at most $k$. The Jacobians and inverse Jacobians are bounded on the compact supports. The product and chain rules therefore bound each localized $H^k$ norm by a constant times the finite-atlas norm in the other chart. Summing over the finite cover gives both norm inequalities. Thus the norms are equivalent and define the same complete Sobolev topology. [given, A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 Localize by the fixed finite partition and extend each compactly supported coefficient by zero into a bounded Euclidean ball. For $p=2$, $2k>d$; [F2] makes each localized $H^k$ coefficient a Banach algebra and gives its $C^1$ representative when $k>d/2+1$. The finite sum of these estimates proves the same algebra and embedding bounds for sections, matrix-valued functions, and forms in the chosen bundle atlas. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 The finite-dimensional matrix exponential is smooth, has derivative the identity at zero on $\mathfrak{su}(N)$, and maps $\mathfrak{su}(N)$ into $SU(N)$. In the Banach algebra from step 2.1 its power series and every termwise derivative converge in $H^{k+1}$ on a sufficiently small ball, since the algebra norm is submultiplicative after an equivalent rescaling. The matrix logarithm series converges on a neighborhood of the identity; for a unitary matrix sufficiently close to identity its logarithm is anti-Hermitian, and its trace is zero because the determinant is one and the sum of the small eigenvalue angles lies in $2\pi\mathbb Z$. Hence pointwise $\exp$ and $\log$ give inverse smooth maps between neighborhoods of zero in $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ and the identity in $\mathcal G_{k+1}$. The inverse-function theorem [F3] also supplies these local Banach charts. Their translated charts cover the group; changes of chart are smooth because the transition functions of $\operatorname{Ad}P$ act by smooth conjugation and the multiplication is a bounded bilinear Sobolev map. The pointwise product and inverse therefore close on $\mathcal G_{k+1}$ and are smooth, giving the asserted Hilbert Lie group. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1]

4.1 In a local trivialization the action is $A^u=u^{-1}Au+u^{-1}du$. Step 2.1 bounds multiplication $H^{k+1}\times H^k\to H^k$ because $H^{k+1}\hookrightarrow H^k$ continuously and $H^k$ is an algebra. Thus the first term is smooth in $(A,u)$. In the charts of step 3.1, inversion is smooth and differentiation $H^{k+1}\to H^k$ is bounded. The derivative of the second term $f(u)=u^{-1}du$ in a tangent direction $\eta$ is $Df(u)[\eta]=-u^{-1}\eta u^{-1}du+u^{-1}d\eta$. Every further derivative is a finite sum of products of $u^{-1}$, tangent factors $\eta_i$, and at most one differentiated tangent factor $d\eta_j$; each product is bounded in $H^k$ by step 2.1. Finite-dimensional Taylor remainders for matrix inversion, multiplied using the same algebra estimate, tend to zero in the required Sobolev norm at every order. Therefore $f$ and the full gauge action are smooth. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For $t\in\mathbb R$, expand in the finite-dimensional matrix algebra: $e^{-t\xi}(A+ta)e^{t\xi}=A+t(a+[A,\xi])+o(t)$ in $H^k$, while $e^{-t\xi}d(e^{t\xi})=t\,d\xi+o(t)$ in $H^k$ by the bounded derivative and product estimates of step 2.1. Adding the two terms gives derivative $a+d\xi+[A,\xi]=a+d_A\xi$, which is the displayed formula. [F1, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

blocks: [F1] The spaces, finite-atlas norms, right-action formula, and irreducibility convention are those of the preceding definition; $H^k$ embeds continuously in $C^1$. [[def-qftx-smooth-sobolev-gauge-configuration]], [[lem-qftx-gauge-sobolev-calculus]]
associated_steps: 1.1 A gauge section $u$ stabilizes $A$ exactly when the local action formula gives $du=uA-Au$, that is, $d_Au=0$. This equation says that $u$ is parallel for the induced connection on $\operatorname{Ad}P$. Since $M$ is connected, parallel transport determines $u$ everywhere from its value at $p_m$, so evaluation is injective on the stabilizer. A parallel section's value commutes with transport around every based loop, hence lies in the holonomy centralizer. [given, A1, F1, algebra]

1.2 Let $B_j=A_j^{u_j}$ and work in the fixed finite atlas. The local action formula gives $du_j=u_jB_j-A_ju_j$. Since $u_j$ is unitary, its pointwise matrix norm is bounded uniformly. The convergent sequences $A_j,B_j$ are bounded in $H^k$, so the equation gives a uniform $H^1$ bound on $u_j$. If a uniform $H^r$ bound holds for some $0\le r\le k$, [F6] bounds both products on the right in $H^r$; hence $du_j$ is bounded in $H^r$ and $u_j$ is bounded in $H^{r+1}$. Induction through $r=k$ gives a uniform $H^{k+1}$ bound. [given, F1, F6, algebra]

2.1 Conversely, let $g\in SU(N)$ commute with every element of $\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)$. Transport $g$ from $p_m$ along any path to a point $x$ and conjugate it by the path's parallel-transport matrix. Two paths give the same value because their concatenation has holonomy commuting with $g$. In local coordinates this gives a parallel section $u$ with $u(p_m)=g$. It is $C^1$ since $A\in H^k\hookrightarrow C^1$ and the parameter-dependent parallel-transport ODE is $C^1$ in the endpoint. The equation $du=uA-Au$, the bounds [F6], and induction on $r=0,1,\ldots,k$ show $u\in H^{k+1}$: starting with its $C^1$ local coefficients, if $u\in H^r$ then the right side is in $H^r$, so all first derivatives are in $H^r$ and $u\in H^{r+1}$. Thus $u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}$ and stabilizes $A$, proving that evaluation has exactly the stated image. [given, F1, F2, F6, step 1.1]

2.2 By [F4], a subsequence converges strongly in $H^k$ to a section $u$. The $H^k\hookrightarrow C^0$ embedding preserves the pointwise $SU(N)$ equations and the bundle transition law, so $u$ is a group-bundle section. In the gauge equation, $A_j\to A$, $B_j\to B$, and $u_j\to u$ in $H^k$; because $H^k$ is an algebra, $u_jB_j-A_ju_j\to uB-Au$ in $H^k$. Thus $du_j$ converges in $H^k$ and the local coefficients converge in $H^{k+1}$. The limit satisfies $du=uB-Au$, equivalently $B=A^u$, and $u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.2]

4.1 For each $1\le r<N$, represent an $r$-plane in $\mathbb C^N$ by its Hermitian orthogonal projection $Q$, so the Grassmannian is $\{Q:Q^*=Q,\ Q^2=Q,\ \operatorname{tr}Q=r\}$ in the finite-dimensional matrix space. Such projections have norm one. Regard any sequence of them as constant curves on $[0,1]$; [F3] gives a uniformly convergent subsequence, and the three defining equations pass to its limit. Thus each Grassmannian is compact. Suppose $A_j\to A$ and each $A_j$ is reducible. A subsequence has a fixed invariant dimension $r$, and by compactness another subsequence of invariant projections converges to $Q$. For every fixed based loop $\gamma$, [F2] and [F1] give $\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A_j,\gamma)\to\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A,\gamma)$. Since the holonomy matrices are unitary and preserve $\operatorname{ran}Q_j$, they commute with $Q_j$; passing to the limit shows that $\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A,\gamma)$ commutes with $Q$ for every loop. Therefore $\operatorname{ran}Q$ is a nonzero proper invariant subspace and $A$ is reducible. The reducible locus is closed, so $\mathcal A_k^*$ is open. [F1, F2, F3, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The action map is continuous by the preceding Sobolev-calculus lemma. For a compact subset of $\mathcal A_k^*\times\mathcal A_k^*$, any sequence in its inverse image has a subsequence whose connection and transformed-connection coordinates converge in that compact set. Steps 1.2 and 2.2 give a further subsequence of gauge classes converging in $\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$, while step 3.1 gives freeness. The inverse image is closed because the action map is continuous, so sequential compactness in these metrizable spaces is compactness. This proves properness. By step 3.1 the reduced action is free. [F1, step 3.1, step 1.2, step 2.2] ∎

blocks: [F1] The covariant derivative and formal adjoint have the local coefficient formulas fixed in the configuration definition. [[def-qftx-smooth-sobolev-gauge-configuration]]
associated_steps: 3.1 If $\Delta_A\xi=0$ for $\xi\in H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$, the formal-adjoint identity, first for smooth approximants and then by Sobolev continuity, gives $0=\langle\Delta_A\xi,\xi\rangle_{L^2}=\|d_A\xi\|_{L^2}^2$. Hence $d_A\xi=0$. Parallel transport makes $\xi$ determined by $\xi(p_m)$, and that value commutes with holonomy. By [F2], $\exp(t\xi(p_m))$ lies in the finite group $Z_N$ for every real $t$, because $\xi(p_m)$ commutes with holonomy. The path is continuous and equals the identity at $t=0$, so it is constant; differentiating at zero gives $\xi(p_m)=0$. Parallel transport then gives $\xi=0$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

6.1 Define $\Pi_A=d_AG_Ad_A^*$. The Sobolev orders give a bounded map $H^k(\Omega^1(\operatorname{ad}P))\to H^k(\Omega^1(\operatorname{ad}P))$. Since $\Delta_A G_A=I$ and $G_A\Delta_A=I$, one has $\Pi_A d_A\xi=d_A\xi$ and $d_A^*(I-\Pi_A)a=0$ for every $\xi\in H^{k+1}$ and $a\in H^k$. Thus $\Pi_A$ is a bounded projection with range $\operatorname{im}d_A$, while $I-\Pi_A$ has range $\ker d_A^*$. Their ranges intersect trivially: if $d_A\xi\in\ker d_A^*$, then $\Delta_A\xi=0$, so step 3.1 gives $\xi=0$. This proves the direct-sum decomposition and projection formula. Smooth dependence of $G_A$, $d_A$, and $d_A^*$ from step 5.1 makes $\Pi_A$ smooth in $A$. [F1, step 3.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

blocks: [F1] The Sobolev connection space is affine, the right gauge action is smooth, and its derivative at $(A,e)$ is $(a,\xi)\mapsto a+d_A\xi$. [[def-qftx-smooth-sobolev-gauge-configuration]], [[lem-qftx-gauge-sobolev-calculus]]
associated_steps: 1.1 The finite center $Z_N$ acts freely on the Banach Lie group $\mathcal G_{k+1}$ by translations. Around any group element choose an open chart whose distinct $Z_N$-translates are disjoint; the quotient map restricts to a chart on each such neighborhood, with transition maps given by smooth translations. Multiplication and inversion descend smoothly, so $\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$ is a Banach Lie group. Since a central gauge section acts trivially on connections, this is the structure group of the reduced action. [A1, F1, algebra]

1.2 The tangent space of the Coulomb slice at $A$ is $\ker d_A^*$. By [F3], the bounded linear map $L_A:\ker d_A^*\oplus H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)\to H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$, $L_A(a,\xi)=a+d_A\xi$, is an isomorphism with inverse $v\mapsto(v-d_AG_Ad_A^*v,G_Ad_A^*v)$. The derivative of $(a,\xi)\mapsto(A+a)^{\exp\xi}$ at $(0,0)$ is $L_A$ by [F1]. [F1, F3]

1.3 Define $F(a,\xi):=d_A^*((A+a)^{\exp\xi}-A)$ for $a\in H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ near $0$ and $\xi\in H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ near $0$. This is a smooth map into $H^{k-1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ by [F1], and $F(0,0)=0$. Its partial derivative in $\xi$ at $(0,0)$ is $d_A^*d_A=\Delta_A$, an isomorphism by [F3]. The implicit-function theorem [F4] therefore gives, for every connection sufficiently near $A$, a unique nearby gauge parameter moving it into the Coulomb condition $d_A^*(B^u-A)=0$. This supplies a local section of the orbit projection. [F1, F3, F4]

2.1 Apply the inverse-function theorem [F4] to $\Phi_A(s,u):=s^u$ on the local Banach product $S_{A,\varepsilon}\times\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$ near $(A,e)$; its derivative is $L_A$ from step 1.2. Shrink $\varepsilon$ so the slice remains in the open irreducible locus. At $(s,e)$, for $s=A+a$, the derivative is $L_s(b,\xi)=b+d_s\xi$ on $b\in\ker d_A^*$; this differs from $L_A$ only by $(b,\xi)\mapsto[a,\xi]$. Its operator norm is at most $C\|a\|_{H^k}$ by [F7]. Choose $\varepsilon$ so $C\varepsilon\|L_A^{-1}\|<1$; then [F5] makes $L_s$ an isomorphism for every $s$ in the slice. At an arbitrary $(s,u_0)$, write $u=u_0v$ near $u_0$ and use $s^{u_0v}=(s^{u_0})^v$. Applying the inverse action by $u_0$ to the target tangent and changing the gauge tangent by the invertible adjoint action identifies this derivative with $L_s$. Hence the derivative is an isomorphism at every point of the slice product, and the inverse-function theorem makes $\Phi_A$ a local diffeomorphism throughout. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F7, step 1.2]

5.1 The orbit relation on $\mathcal A_k^*$ is closed: if $x_j^{u_j}=y_j$ and $(x_j,y_j)\to(x,y)$, properness [F2] gives a convergent subsequence $u_{j_\ell}\to u$, and continuity of the action gives $x^u=y$. For distinct orbits, the complement of this closed relation contains their pair, so there are product neighborhoods $O_x\times O_y$ disjoint from the relation. Their saturations are open and disjoint: if the saturations intersected, some translate of a point in $O_x$ would equal a translate of a point in $O_y$, making that pair related. Their quotient images therefore separate the two orbits. This proves the quotient is Hausdorff. [F1, F2, step 4.1]

5.2 For the smooth-space clause, fix now a smooth irreducible center $A\in\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and use the Banach slice and trivialization established in step 4.1. Put $U_A=\Phi_A(S_{A,\varepsilon}\times\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1})$ and $V_A=\pi_k(S_{A,\varepsilon})$. Since $U_A$ is open in $\mathcal A_k^*$, $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open in the stated $C^\infty$ topology; set $S_A^\infty=S_{A,\varepsilon}\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and $V_A^\infty=\pi_\infty(S_A^\infty)$. For a smooth $B\in U_A$, its unique reduced gauge class from step 4.1 has a representative $u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}$. It satisfies $d_A^*(B^{u^{-1}}-A)=0$. Locally in a bundle frame, write $C_j=uB_j u^{-1}-(\partial_j u)u^{-1}-A_j$. Substitution in $d_A^*C=0$, use of $\partial_i(u^{-1})=-u^{-1}(\partial_i u)u^{-1}$, and multiplication on the right by $u$ isolate the equation $g^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j u=R(A,B,g;u,u^{-1},du)$ on each chart. Every term in $R$ is a finite product of smooth coefficients (including first derivatives of $A,B$) and factors among $u,u^{-1},du$; hence the principal operator is the scalar smooth Laplacian on each matrix entry. If $u\in H^{r+1}$ for $r\ge k$, then this right-hand side lies in $H^r$ by [F7] and the smooth coefficient bounds. Elliptic regularity [F6] gives $u\in H^{r+2}$. Iteration proves $u$ smooth; changing its representative by an element of the finite center preserves smoothness. Thus every smooth point of the Banach saturation has a smooth trivialization representative, and $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*=\pi_\infty^{-1}(V_A^\infty)$. [F1, F2, F6, F7, step 4.1]

6.1 Suppose smooth $B_j\to B$ in $C^\infty$ within $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$. The Banach trivialization from step 4.1 gives convergence of their slice representatives in $H^k$ and of their reduced gauge classes in $H^{k+1}$. In a quotient chart around the limiting class from step 1.1, choose lifts $u_j,u$ that converge in $H^{k+1}$; this is possible because the finite center acts by disjoint translates. The equation in step 5.2 and elliptic estimates [F6] bootstrap convergence: if $u_j\to u$ in $H^{r+1}$, then the assumed $C^\infty$ convergence gives $B_j\to B$ in $H^{r+1}$, and [F7] makes the right-hand sides converge in $H^r$. Apply the elliptic estimate to $u_j-u$, using also their already known $H^{k+1}$ convergence for the $L^2$ term, to get $u_j\to u$ in $H^{r+2}$. Induction gives convergence in every Sobolev order, which on compact $M$ is the $C^\infty$ section topology. The slice representatives converge in $C^\infty$ by their action formula. Conversely the forward action is continuous in the $C^\infty$ topology by multiplication and differentiation of smooth sections. The saturation $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open, and $V_A^\infty$ is open in the quotient because the quotient map is open: the saturation of any open set is a union of its open gauge translates. The restricted map $S_A^\infty\times\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty\to\pi_\infty^{-1}(V_A^\infty)$ is therefore a homeomorphism for the actual quotient topology, and it is equivariant. This proves the smooth-space topological principal bundle claim. [F1, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 5.2] ∎

blocks: [F1] [[def-qftx-smooth-sobolev-gauge-configuration]] fixes $p_m$, $\mathcal G_{k+1,m}$, $Z_N$, $\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$, and the right-action convention $A^u=u^{-1}Au+u^{-1}du$.
associated_steps: 1.1 If $u$ is in the stabilizer, its value $u(p_m)$ is in the holonomy centralizer by [F2]. Conversely, [F2] says each centralizing value extends uniquely by parallel transport to a stabilizing gauge section. Thus evaluation is a bijection between the stabilizer and the centralizer. In particular, when $u(p_m)=e$, parallel transport gives $u=e$ everywhere, proving the based stabilizer is trivial without irreducibility. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 If $A$ is irreducible, [F2] identifies the full stabilizer with $Z_N$. Every element of this center is divided out in $\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$, so the reduced stabilizer consists only of the identity coset. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

blocks: [F1] [[def-qftx-smooth-sobolev-gauge-configuration]] fixes the Sobolev spaces and right-action convention. [[lem-qftx-gauge-sobolev-calculus]] gives the differential $D\Phi_A(0,0)(a,\xi)=a+d_A\xi$.
associated_steps: 1.1 The calculus lemma [F1] differentiates the right-action formula at the identity, giving $D\Phi_A(0,0)(a,\xi)=a+d_A\xi$. Its domain is $\ker d_A^*\oplus H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ and its codomain is $H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$. The gauge derivative $d_A:H^{k+1}\to H^k$ explains the one-derivative loss. [A1, F1, algebra]

associated_steps: 1.1 By [F1], $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is exactly the set of connections whose holonomy action has no common proper nonzero invariant subspace. By [F2], for each such connection the stabilizer in the stated Sobolev gauge group is $Z_N$. The latter is the conditional stabilizer conclusion recorded separately from the holonomy criterion. [A1, given, F1, F2]

1.2 For each $V\in\mathscr G_N$, irreducibility supplies a based piecewise-smooth loop $\ell_V$ whose holonomy $g_V=\operatorname{Hol}_A(\ell_V)$ does not preserve $V$. If $P_V$ is the orthogonal projection onto $V$, then $(I-P_V)g_VP_V\ne0$. For each fixed loop $\ell$, the set of $V$ with $(I-P_V)\operatorname{Hol}_A(\ell)P_V\ne0$ is open, since the projector topology and matrix multiplication are continuous. These open sets cover $\mathscr G_N$. [F1, F3, given, construct]

6.1 A $C^1$ neighborhood on the compact base is specified by finitely many continuous section seminorms; each is continuous in the $C^\infty$ section topology. Therefore the neighborhood in step 4.1 is also a $C^\infty$ neighborhood, and $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open. step 2.1 gives the finite holonomy witness at $A$, and step 1.1 gives the stated stabilizer. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎
