associated_steps: 1.1 If $K=\varnothing$ or $f(K)\subseteq\mathcal A_\infty^*$, the constant homotopy suffices. Otherwise realize the given finite simplicial complex by its barycentric coordinates as a compact subset of $\mathbb R^q$, taking $q\ge1$. Let $U=f^{-1}(\mathcal A_\infty^*)$, an open neighborhood of $L$ by [F2]. Choose nested relatively open neighborhoods $U_0,U_1,U_2$ of $L$ in $K$ with $\overline U_0\subset U_1$, $\overline U_1\subset U_2$, and $\overline U_2\subset U$; if $L=\varnothing$ take them empty. The compact family $f(\overline U_2)$ is uniformly stable under a sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbation: each member has the finite-loop positive margin in [F2], and a finite subcover gives one positive tolerance. Include this $C^1$ norm among the finitely many seminorms in which all forthcoming approximations are to be small. [A1, F1, F2, given, cases, construct]

2.1 Fix a small positive tolerance $\delta$ in each of those seminorms. Uniform continuity on compact $K$ gives a radius $\rho>0$ so that $f(s_i)-f(s)$ is smaller than $\delta$ in every selected seminorm when $s,s_i\in K$ and $|s-s_i|<2\rho$. Choose finitely many $s_i\in K$ with the balls $B_\rho(s_i)$ covering $K$. Let $\psi_i$ be nonnegative smooth ambient bumps supported in $B_{2\rho}(s_i)$ and positive on $B_\rho(s_i)$, constructed by translating and rescaling $\exp(-1/(1-|x|^2))$ on the unit ball and extending by zero. On the open neighborhood $V=\{\sum_i\psi_i>0\}$ of $K$, put $\lambda_i=\psi_i/\sum_j\psi_j$ and $g(s)=A_0+\sum_i\lambda_i(s)(f(s_i)-A_0)$. This is an ambient smooth finite-affine family of smooth connections. For $s\in K$, every contributing sample is within $2\rho$ of $s$, so $p(g(s)-f(s))<\delta$ for each selected seminorm $p$. This construction smooths the parameter dependence directly and simultaneously on the whole polyhedron; it changes no face independently of its cofaces. [F1, F6, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Choose a smooth ambient cutoff $0\le\theta\le1$ which is zero on a neighborhood of $\overline U_0$ and one on a neighborhood of the disjoint compact set $K\setminus U_1$. Such a cutoff follows from finitely many ambient bumps separating the two compact sets. Define on $K$ the continuous family $h(s)=f(s)+\theta(s)(g(s)-f(s))$. The straight interpolation from $f$ to $h$ is fixed near $L$ and is $\delta$-small in every selected seminorm. By the uniform $C^1$ margin in step 1.1, choosing $\delta$ small ensures it is irreducible on $\overline U_2$. Its closed reducible-parameter set $R=\{s\in K:h(s)\notin\mathcal A_\infty^*\}$ is compact and contained in $K\setminus U_2$, hence in the ambient open region where $\theta=1$ and $h=g$ on $K$. If $R$ is empty the first interpolation already proves the result. Otherwise choose an ambient open $W$ with compact closure in $V\cap\{\theta=1\}$, containing $R$ and avoiding a neighborhood of $L$, and a smooth cutoff $0\le\chi\le1$ with compact support $T\subset W$, positive on $R$. All subsequent holonomy calculations use the ambient family $g$ on $W$; on the actual parameter subset $K\cap W$ this is exactly $h$. [F1, F2, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

5.1 Let $U_i(s,t)$ be parallel transport for $g(s)$ from the chosen base frame to a point at parameter $t$ of $\ell_i$. It is smooth in $s\in W$ and in $t$ on each segment by [F4], applied on finitely many common intervals along the compact loop. In tube coordinates $(t,z)$ around its private arc, choose a bump $\rho_i(t)$ of integral one supported away from the arc ends, a transverse bump $c(z)$ with $c(0)=1$, and a real basis $X_a$ of $\mathfrak{su}(N)$. In a fixed smooth frame on the tube define the adjoint-valued form $b_{i,a}(s)=\rho_i(t)c(z)U_i(s,t)X_aU_i(s,t)^{-1}\,dt$, extending its coefficients constantly in the transverse coordinates before multiplying by $c$ and extending by zero outside the tube. It is a genuine smooth bundle-valued one-form depending smoothly on the ambient parameter. Along the loop its contraction is exactly the displayed transported Lie-algebra element. [F1, F4, step 4.1, construct]

10.1 Define on all of $K$ the final family $h_v(s)=h(s)+\chi(s)\sum_{j,a}v_{j,a}b_{j,a}(s)$, with the added term zero off $W$. The compact support $T$ and its spatial smoothness make this term continuous in every section seminorm, and its value uniformly small in any specified finite list by taking $v$ sufficiently small. If $\chi(s)>0$, then $s\in W$ and $h(s)=g(s)$, so $h_v(s)$ has the holonomy tuple $\Phi(s,v)$, which has no common invariant proper subspace by step 9.1. Therefore $h_v(s)$ is irreducible. If $\chi(s)=0$, then $s\notin R$ since $\chi$ is positive on $R$, so $h_v(s)=h(s)$ was already irreducible. The straight perturbation homotopy from $h$ to $h_v$ is fixed on an open neighborhood of $L$. Concatenate it with the interpolation in step 3.1. Choose $\delta$ and then $v$ within half of each requested seminorm tolerance; the triangle inequality gives the asserted bounds relative to the original $f$ for the entire concatenated homotopy. All formulas are global on $K$, so faces and cofaces agree automatically. [F1, F2, F9, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 9.1, construct, algebra] ∎

blocks: [F1] The batch-56 configuration definition sets $\mathcal A_\infty=A_0+\Omega^1(M;\operatorname{ad}P)$ and defines $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ by irreducibility of the based holonomy action on $\mathbb C^N$. Its complete definition was inspected and its current Step 1 record is ready; the argument uses exactly this interface ([[def-qftx-smooth-sobolev-gauge-configuration]]).
associated_steps: 1.1 The affine space $\mathcal A_\infty$ contains $A_0$. Apply [F2] to the constant map from a one-point polyhedron with empty subpolyhedron and value $A_0$. Its endpoint is an element of $\mathcal A_\infty^*$, proving nonemptiness. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

1.2 Let $A,B\in\mathcal A_\infty^*$. The affine path $\gamma(t)=(1-t)A+tB$ is continuous in the Fréchet topology and has irreducible endpoints. Apply [F2] with $K=I$ and $L=\{0,1\}$. The resulting endpoint path remains in $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and fixes both endpoints, so the locus is path-connected. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]

1.3 Fix $j\ge1$ and a based representative $u:(I^j,\partial I^j)\to(\mathcal A_\infty^*,A)$. The quotient $I^j/\partial I^j$ is homeomorphic to $S^j$, so regard $u$ as a continuous sphere map with value $A$ at the collapsed boundary point. Identify $D^{j+1}$ with the cone on $S^j$ and define $F([r,x])=A_0+r(u(x)-A_0)$ for $0\le r\le1$. For each continuous section seminorm $p$, compactness of $S^j$ gives $C_p=\sup_x p(u(x)-A_0)<\infty$; hence $p(F([r,x])-A_0)\le rC_p\to0$ as $r\to0$. This proves continuity at the cone apex in every defining seminorm, and away from the apex continuity follows from continuity of $u$ and affine operations. Thus $F:D^{j+1}\to\mathcal A_\infty$ is a continuous filling of $u$. [F1, F3, given, algebra, construct]

blocks: [F1] In the trivialization $P=M\times SU(N)$, the affine connection space is $\Omega^1(M;\mathfrak{su}(N))$ translated by the product connection, and the product connection has identity holonomy around every loop ([[def-qftx-smooth-sobolev-gauge-configuration]]).
associated_steps: 1.1 The zero connection has parallel transport equal to the identity in the product trivialization, so its based holonomy group is $\{I_N\}$. Since $N\ge2$, every complex line in $\mathbb C^N$ is a nonzero proper subspace invariant under $I_N$. Thus $0\notin\mathcal A_\infty^*$. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 The cone $D^{j+1}=CS^j$ identifies all $(0,x)$ to one apex and has boundary parameter $r=1$. The formula $F([r,x])=r f(x)$ is well-defined because it is independent of $x$ at $r=0$, and equals $f(x)$ at $r=1$. For every continuous section seminorm $p$, compactness of $S^j$ gives $C_p=\sup_x p(f(x))<\infty$, so $p(F([r,x]))\le rC_p\to0$ as $r\to0$. Away from the apex, continuity follows from continuity of $f$ and scalar multiplication in the Fréchet vector space. Hence $F$ is a continuous affine filling in $\mathcal A_\infty$. [F1, given, algebra, construct]

blocks: [F1] The current configuration carrier defines $\operatorname{Ad}P=P\times_{Ad}SU(N)$, the smooth gauge group $\mathcal G_\infty$ with finite-atlas $C^\infty$ derivative seminorms, the based subgroup $\mathcal G_{k+1,m}=\{u:u(p_m)=e\}$ at Sobolev regularity, and the chosen frame $p_m$; it assumes compact connected oriented boundaryless $M$ of dimension $3$ or $4$, $N\ge2$, and full AC. associated_steps: 1.1 Realize $Ad(P)$ as the associated bundle with fiber $SU(N)$ under conjugation and embed that fiber in the real vector space of complex matrices with its Hilbert–Schmidt norm. The associated matrix bundle has linear conjugation transition functions. A continuous family of sections parametrized by a compact smooth pair $(X,K)$ is a continuous family of sections of this matrix bundle; on $K$ it is continuous in the $C^\infty$ topology. Apply [F2], using the fixed basepoint value $I$ as a marked fiber value in the based case, to obtain a uniformly close matrix-valued smooth-section family, unchanged on $K$ and at that point. [F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 The compact matrix submanifold $SU(N)$ has a positive-radius tubular neighborhood by [F3]. The Hilbert–Schmidt metric is invariant under conjugation by $SU(N)$; uniqueness of the nearest point therefore makes the retraction equivariant under every transition function of $Ad(P)$. Choose the approximation in step 1.1 closer than half the tubular radius and compose it fiberwise with this retraction. The result is a family of smooth $SU(N)$-sections, continuous in the $C^\infty$ topology; it still agrees with the original family on $K$ and at the fixed fiber value because the retraction fixes $SU(N)$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

4.1 For surjectivity on $\pi_j$ with $j\ge1$, take a continuous sphere family $f:S^j\to\mathcal G^0(P)$ based at the identity section and apply steps 1.1–3.1 with empty relative boundary, obtaining a homotopy $F_t$ to a family continuous into the smooth-section topology. If $x_0$ is the parameter basepoint, normalize this entire homotopy by $\widehat F_t(x)=F_t(x_0)^{-1}F_t(x)$. Its initial family is $f$, its value at $x_0$ is the identity for every $t$, and its endpoint is continuous in the smooth-section topology because multiplication and inversion there are continuous. In the based spatial subgroup this normalization also preserves the value $I$ at the marked fiber. Thus the smooth representative and its comparison homotopy are genuinely based in the parameter variable. For injectivity, a nullhomotopy in the continuous group is a family $H:D^{j+1}\to\mathcal G^0(P)$ whose restriction to $S^j$ is the given smooth-topology family; apply the relative construction with $K=S^j$ to make the extension smooth in the section variable while fixing its boundary. Choose the basepoint $x_0\in S^j$ on the boundary and identify the disk with the unit ball; the contraction $R_t(x)=(1-t)x+t x_0$ fixes $x_0$ and contracts the boundary into the disk's interior. Then $H(R_t(x))$ is a based nullhomotopy because its value at $x_0$ is the fixed boundary value $e$. Thus injectivity holds in based homotopy groups, not only free homotopy classes. For path components, approximate a single section for surjectivity; for injectivity, approximate a continuous path relative to its two smooth endpoints using $X=I$ and its collared boundary $K=\{0,1\}$. These constructions give the component bijection without imposing identity normalization on arbitrary components. In the based subgroup, mark the chosen fiber and preserve the value $I$ throughout. Pointwise multiplication and inversion on $\mathcal G_\infty$ are continuous in its $C^\infty$ topology: in each finite-atlas chart the product rule and chain rule bound each derivative seminorm by finitely many seminorms of the inputs. The compact-open section group is also a topological group because $SU(N)$ multiplication and inversion are continuous and $M$ is compact. Thus translations in both groups are homeomorphisms and transfer the identity-based conclusion to every basepoint. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

It also defines the Sobolev spaces, $\mathcal A_\infty$, and $\overline{\mathcal G}_\infty=\mathcal G_\infty/Z_N$. associated_steps: 1.2 The finite group $Z_N$ acts on the Hausdorff topological group $\mathcal G(P)$ by free translations. Choose an identity neighborhood $V$ with $V^{-1}V\cap Z_N=\{e\}$; this is possible because the finite set $Z_N\setminus\{e\}$ is closed and avoids the identity. The translates $Vz$ are pairwise disjoint. Since the quotient map is open and identifies each translate homeomorphically with the image of $V$, that image is evenly covered. Translation gives the same construction around every group element, so the quotient map is a covering with exactly $|Z_N|=N$ sheets. By [F1] and [A1], this is the finite-center quotient specified in the Statement. [A1, F1, given]

2.1 In the finite-atlas $C^\infty$ topology, pointwise multiplication and inversion are continuous: each derivative seminorm of a product or inverse is bounded on compact chart supports by finitely many derivative seminorms of the inputs, by the finite-dimensional product and chain rules. If $s:U\to\mathcal G(P)$ is one of the local sections, the maps
$$(v,g)\longmapsto v\,s(g),\qquad u\longmapsto\bigl(u\,s(ev_m(u))^{-1},ev_m(u)\bigr)$$
are continuous inverses between $\mathcal G_m(P)\times U$ and $ev_m^{-1}(U)$. The first coordinate in the inverse evaluates to $e$, and the product reconstructs $u$. Thus evaluation is a locally trivial bundle with fiber exactly its kernel $\mathcal G_m(P)$. A finite cover of compact $SU(N)$ by such neighborhoods and a partition of unity make this bundle numerable. By [F2] it is a Hurewicz fibration; [F3] supplies its homotopy LES. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

associated_steps:
1.1 By [F1], the gauge group under consideration consists of smooth sections with value $e$ at $p_m$, and [F3] identifies this subgroup with the evaluation fiber and its subspace topology. First calculate its continuous-section model, which is related by [F2]. Hemisphere trivializations exist directly from the supplied smooth reference connection: choose a frame at the center of each closed disk and transport it along its radial segments. The ODE statement [F6] gives a smooth section up to the equator, including the disk center, and the two sections give the smooth transition $\psi$ in [A1]. In that model a based section is a pair of maps $f_+:D_+^r\to SU(N)$ and $f_-:D_-^r\to SU(N)$ satisfying [A1] and $f_+(m)=e$. Let $J=\operatorname{Map}_*((D_+^r,m),(SU(N),e))$. For $f\in J$ define a map on the lower disk by
$$\sigma_f(\rho q)=\psi(q)^{-1}f(\rho q)\psi(q),\quad 0<\rho\le1,\qquad \sigma_f(0)=e,$$
where $q\in S^{r-1}$ is the radial direction and the upper-disk center $m$ is identified with $0$. At $\rho=1$ this has boundary value $\psi^{-1}f(q)\psi$, and as $\rho\to0$ it tends uniformly to $e$ because $f(0)=e$ and $S^{r-1}$ is compact; hence it is continuous on $D_-^r$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F6, construct]

associated_steps:
1.1 Suppose $r=3$. By [F3, F4], $\pi_0(\mathcal G_m(P))\cong\pi_3(SU(N))\cong\mathbb Z$. The evaluation LES [F2, F6] has the component segment
$$\pi_1(SU(N))\longrightarrow\pi_0(\mathcal G_m(P))\longrightarrow\pi_0(\mathcal G(P))\longrightarrow\pi_0(SU(N)).$$
The outer terms are one-point sets by [F4]. The induced map on components is surjective by exactness, and its fibers are the orbits of $\pi_1(SU(N))$ on $\pi_0(\mathcal G_m(P))$ in the action clause of [F6]. That acting group is trivial, so each fiber is a singleton and the middle map is a bijection. Thus $\mathcal G(P)$ has infinitely many components. Since $\mathcal G(P)\to\overline{\mathcal G}(P)$ is a covering with $N$ sheets, components downstairs correspond to orbits of the finite deck group on components upstairs: a path downstairs lifts by [F7] to a path whose endpoint differs from its starting lift by one deck transformation, and each deck orbit is therefore one quotient component. Each orbit has at most $N$ elements, so infinitely many components remain. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, F7]

associated_steps: 2.1 The evaluation fibration has connected base $SU(2)$ and $\pi_1(SU(2))=0$ by [F2, F3]. Its component LES therefore identifies $\pi_0(\mathcal G_m)$ with $\pi_0(\mathcal G)$, so the full group also has infinitely many components. The quotient by $Z_2$ is a two-sheeted covering; [F6] shows its components are the orbits of the two-element deck action on the components upstairs. Each orbit has at most two members, so an infinite component set remains infinite after quotient; this instance is also the $r=3,N=2$ case of [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, algebra] ∎

blocks: [F3] The preceding lemma supplies the exact P² diagonal monad and its framed vanishings under the stated cohomology/base-change assumptions; its algebraic/analytic family comparison uses the exact projective GAGA interface and the stated base-change hypotheses. [[lem-qftx-p2-beilinson-diagonal-and-framed-vanishing]]
associated_steps: 1.2 Conversely, let $\mathcal E$ be a framed torsion-free sheaf with the stated Hilbert polynomial. The preceding Beilinson lemma constructs its monad, with terms $V_1\mathcal O(-1)$, $M\mathcal O$, and $V_2\mathcal O(1)$ of ranks $k,2k+N,k$. Its restriction to $L_\infty$ remains exact at the ends because $\mathcal E$ is locally free there. Put $K=\ker\beta|_{L_\infty}$. The sequence $0\to V_1\mathcal O(-1)\to K\to W\mathcal O\to0$ splits since $\operatorname{Ext}^1(W\mathcal O,V_1\mathcal O(-1))=V_1\otimes W^*\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-1))=0$. [F3, F5]

2.3 The remaining line extension $0\to V_1\mathcal O(-1)\oplus W\mathcal O\to M\mathcal O\to V_2\mathcal O(1)\to0$ has class in $\operatorname{Hom}(V_2,V_1)\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-2))$, since $H^1(\mathcal O(-1))=0$. Twist by $\mathcal O(-1)$ and take cohomology. The connecting map $V_2\to V_1\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-2))$ is an isomorphism: the adjacent groups $H^0(\mathcal O(-1))$ and $H^1(\mathcal O(-1))$ vanish, while $H^1(\mathcal O(-2))\cong\mathbb C$. Thus $V_2$ is identified with $V_1$ by this canonical extension class. Choosing a basis of $V_1$ and using the fixed framed basis of $W$ identifies $M=V\oplus V\oplus W$ and the line maps with the two Euler blocks in the Statement. Any other such choice differs by one simultaneous element of $GL(V)$. [F3, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

3.2 The remaining coefficients of the two linear maps are their $z_0$ coefficients, so write $\alpha=(z_0B_1-z_1,z_0B_2-z_2,z_0J)^T$ and $\beta=(-z_0C_1+z_2,z_0C_2-z_1,z_0I)$. The coefficients of $z_0z_1$ and $z_0z_2$ in $\beta\alpha=0$ force $C_1=B_2$ and $C_2=B_1$; the $z_0^2$ coefficient is then $[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$. This recovers the stated ADHM form. The surjectivity of $\beta$ implies stability: if $U=\operatorname{span}\{B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(W)\}$ were proper, it is invariant and the induced $B_1,B_2$ on $V/U$ commute because $[B_1,B_2]=-IJ$ has image in $U$. Their dual actions on the nonzero annihilator $U^\perp\subset V^*$ commute, so [F6] gives a common eigen-covector $\lambda\ne0$ with $\lambda I=0$. At the corresponding affine point, $\lambda\beta=0$, contradicting surjectivity. [F1, F3, F6, step 2.1, step 2.3, algebra]

4.2 The Beilinson construction is natural under framed sheaf isomorphisms, so an isomorphism of framed sheaves induces maps on the cohomology vector spaces used in steps 1.2–6.2 and hence a single change of basis $g\in GL(V)$; the normalized Euler blocks force the recovered tuples to differ by $g\cdot(B_1,B_2,I,J)$. Conversely such a $g$ is an isomorphism of monads acting trivially on $W$, and therefore induces a framed sheaf isomorphism. This proves the pointwise inverse equivalence modulo $GL(V)$. For a finite-type data family, step 2.1 makes $\beta$ surjective on the total space, so $K=\ker\beta$ is locally free. The sequence $0\to V\mathcal O(-1)\to K\to\mathcal E\to0$ is exact and its terms before $\mathcal E$ are flat over the base. After tensoring with any residue field of the base, the first map remains sheaf-injective by step 1.1; hence $\operatorname{Tor}_1(k(s),\mathcal E)=0$. Since $\mathcal E$ is finite over each local ring of $\mathbb P^2\times S$ and its residue fiber is a vector space over the residue field, [F8] gives flatness over $S$. Under the stated relative cohomology and base-change hypotheses, the same constructions use vector bundles and are inverse for families. [F2, F3, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 2.3, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 Apply the family equivalence to $S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$. A first-order deformation of the ADHM data is $(\dot B_1,\dot B_2,\dot I,\dot J)$ satisfying $d\mu_{\mathbb C}=0$; infinitesimal changes of basis are $d_0(\xi)=([\xi,B_1],[\xi,B_2],\xi I,-J\xi)$. Differentiating the monad gives the chain perturbation $(\dot\alpha,\dot\beta)$ with $\beta\dot\alpha+\dot\beta\alpha=0$, and a change by $d_0(\xi)$ is the corresponding chain homotopy. Since the family construction and its inverse commute with this dual-number base change, they induce inverse linear maps on first-order framed deformations and on the quotient tangent spaces $\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_0$. [F2, F3, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 If $k=0$, $V=0$, all four maps and both equations are the unique zero-dimensional maps, stability and costability are vacuous, and the monad is $0\to W\mathcal O\to0$. Its middle cohomology is the framed bundle $W\mathcal O$ with Hilbert polynomial $N\binom{m+2}{2}$. Conversely, [F3] constructs this same zero-term monad from every framed sheaf with that polynomial, so the framing identifies each such sheaf with $W\mathcal O$. Thus both moduli spaces are points, and all empty-matrix and Euler-block conventions are satisfied. [F1, F3, F5, algebra] ∎

1.2 In the algebraic Chow ring, [F1] and $H=c_1(\mathcal O(1))$ give

[F3] For a stable complex datum the framed $\mathbb P^2$ monad has maps $\alpha=(z_0B_1-z_1,z_0B_2-z_2,z_0J)^T$ and $\beta=(-z_0B_2+z_2,z_0B_1-z_1,z_0I)$, and its middle cohomology is a framed torsion-free sheaf; local freeness is equivalent to costability. associated_steps: 2.1 Substituting that representative in [F3] gives $\alpha=(-z_1,-z_2,0)^T$ and $\beta=(z_2,-z_1,z_0)$. Their product is $-z_2z_1+z_1z_2=0$. The row $\beta$ is surjective at every projective point because its three entries have no common zero, and $\alpha$ is injective as a sheaf map because it is nonzero away from $p$. Let $K=\ker\beta$. Projection to the third coordinate restricts to a morphism $\gamma:K\to\mathcal O$. On the affine chart $z_0=1$, put $x=z_1$ and $y=z_2$; a vector in $K$ has the form $(u,v,-yu+xv)$, so $\gamma(K)=(x,y)$ and its kernel is generated by $(-x,-y,0)$, the image of $\alpha$. On any chart away from $p$ where $z_1$ or $z_2$ is a unit, the same equations show that $\gamma$ is onto and its kernel is generated by $\alpha$. Hence $K/\operatorname{im}\alpha\cong I_p$ globally, where $I_p$ is the ideal sheaf of $p$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 At $p$, the local ideal $(x,y)$ is not principal: if it were generated by one element in the regular local ring $\mathbb C[x,y]_{(x,y)}$, its quotient by the maximal ideal would have dimension at most one, whereas $(x,y)/(x,y)^2$ has dimension two. Therefore $I_p$ is not locally free at $p$. Its framing on $L_\infty$ is the canonical trivialization because $p\notin L_\infty$. This exhibits a positive-FI stable point outside the costable, locally-free zero-FI locus; the correspondence with ordinary ASD moduli is restricted to that zero-FI locus and does not absorb this boundary point. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

[F2] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is the quotient topological group, each class has a representative in $[0,1)$, it is compact Hausdorff and second-countable, and its quotient map is open. [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]
associated_steps:
1.1 By [A1], for any sequence $(A_n)$ of nonempty sets the family
$\mathcal F=\{A_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ has a choice function $g$. The composite
$n\mapsto g(A_n)$ is an indexed selector, even if some sets $A_n$ repeat.
Thus [F1] holds and supplies the countable-choice premise in the quotient
circle definition [F2]. [A1, F1, F2, construct]

1.2 For one factor, [F2] makes each quotient interval $q(I)$ open because
$q$ is open, and $q|_I$ is injective because $I$ has length less than $1$.
Its inverse chart is continuous: $q|_I$ is a continuous open bijection onto
$q(I)$. These charts cover the circle. If two charts overlap, local lifts
differ by an integer; this integer is locally constant, so each transition
map is locally a translation and hence smooth. The charts therefore define a
smooth one-manifold without boundary compatible with the quotient topology.
[F2, construct]

1.3 Addition and inversion on one factor are smooth in these charts. Near any
pair of points, choose local real lifts $x,y$ and an output chart around their
sum; after shrinking the input intervals, the coordinate expression for
addition is $x+y$ plus one fixed integer. Near any point, choose local lifts
for it and its inverse; the coordinate expression for inversion is $-x$ plus
one fixed integer. Both expressions are smooth. With the group law already
given by [F2], this is a Lie group by [F6]. Its underlying circle is compact,
Hausdorff and connected by [F2] and [F3], and it is abelian by the quotient
addition law. [F2, F3, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 The circle has a finite CW structure with one vertex $[0]$ and one open
$1$-cell, the image of $(0,1)$; its characteristic interval has both
endpoints attached to that vertex. For $T$, index product cells by subsets
$J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}$: coordinates in $J$ lie in the open $1$-cell and
all other coordinates equal $[0]$. Each cell is an open cube of dimension
$|J|$, its closure meets only cells indexed by subsets of $J$, and its
characteristic cube is the product of the factor characteristic intervals;
identify each closed cube with a closed disk of the same dimension. The map
$q^r:[0,1]^r\to T$ is a continuous surjection because every coordinate class
has a representative in $[0,1]$ by [F2]. If $K$ is closed in the cube,
then $K$ is compact, $q^r(K)$ is compact, and $q^r(K)$ is closed because $T$
is Hausdorff by [F2] and [F3]. Thus $q^r$ is a quotient map. It is the
characteristic map for the top cell. Every lower-cell characteristic cube is
obtained by precomposing $q^r$ with the continuous coordinate insertion that
fixes omitted coordinates at $0$, so the quotient topology of $q^r$ already
makes every characteristic map continuous; conversely $q^r$ is itself one of
those maps. Hence this quotient topology is exactly the weak topology
determined by the finitely many characteristic cubes. This gives a finite CW
structure with the identity as a $0$-cell. The singleton
identity is a subcomplex, so [F7] gives the homotopy extension property for
its inclusion. [F2, F3, F7, step 2.1, construct]

blocks: [F2] The product torus is compact and has a normalized translation-invariant probability measure, constructed from Lebesgue measure on a product fundamental cube. [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]
associated_steps:
1.1 Choose a smooth Riemannian metric $g_0$ by [F3], let $\mu$ be the normalized Haar probability measure from [F2], and define
$$
g_p(v,w):=\int_T (g_0)_{t^{-1}p}\bigl((d a_{t^{-1}})_p v,(d a_{t^{-1}})_p w\bigr)\,d\mu(t)
$$
for $p\in M$ and $v,w\in T_pM$. [A1, F2, F3, construct]

1.2 In every pair of local tangent-bundle frames the integrand in step 1.1 is smooth in $p$ and the torus coordinates; repeated application of [F4] on $[0,1]^r$ shows that the coefficients of $g$ are smooth. Each integrand is a symmetric bilinear form, and for $v\ne0$ its value on $(v,v)$ is strictly positive because $d a_{t^{-1}}$ is invertible. Its continuous positive value has a positive minimum on compact $T$ by [F5], so the integral is positive and $g$ is a Riemannian metric. For $s\in T$, translation invariance of $\mu$, with the change of variable $t=su$, gives $g_{sp}(d a_s v,d a_s w)=g_p(v,w)$. Thus $g$ is $T$-invariant. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The orthogonal complement $
u_{F,p}=(T_pF)^\perp$ has no fixed vector, since the fixed subspace is precisely $T_pF$ by step 2.2. Complexify $
u_{F,p}$; the commuting orthogonal transformations $ho_p(t)$ become commuting unitary transformations, so simultaneous diagonalization decomposes the complexified fiber into character eigenspaces. Every character is nontrivial because the fixed eigenspace has been removed. A self-inverse character of the connected group $T$ has image in $\{1,-1\}$ and is therefore trivial; hence complex conjugation pairs the remaining $\chi$ and $\chi^{-1}$ eigenspaces. Using the fixed lattice identification, retain the character whose first nonzero integer coordinate is positive from each pair; this equips the real normal fiber with a $T$-invariant complex structure and orientation. For a character $\chi$, the operator $P_\chi=\int_T\overline{\chi(t)}ho_p(t)\,d\mu(t)$ is the orthogonal projection onto its $\chi$-eigenspace: on a $\psi$-eigenvector it acts by the scalar $\int_T\overline{\chi(t)}\psi(t)\,d\mu(t)$. If $\psi=\chi$, this integral is $1$. If $\psi
e\chi$, then $	heta=\overline\chi\psi$ is a nontrivial character; choose $t_0\in T$ with $	heta(t_0)
e1$. Translation invariance gives $I=\int_T	heta(t)\,d\mu(t)=\int_T	heta(t_0t)\,d\mu(t)=	heta(t_0)I$, so $I=0$. The character averages are therefore exactly the eigenspace projections. Their coefficients vary smoothly with $p$ by [F4]. Their ranks are integer-valued and continuous, hence locally constant, so they form smooth subbundles. At each $p$, finitely many weight projections have ranks summing to the full fiber dimension; their ranks remain constant on a neighborhood, leaving no dimension for any other weight there. Thus the finite weight list is locally constant, and compactness of $F$ gives a finite cover by such neighborhoods, so only finitely many weights occur globally. [F2, F4, step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 If $r=0$, the action is trivial, $F=M$, and $\nu_F=0$, so the weight assertion is vacuous. If $M$ is empty, all asserted submanifolds and bundles are empty. Otherwise the construction applies componentwise and uses no assumption on connectedness of $M$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, F7, F8, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

blocks: [[texp-aqft-finite-heavy-scalar-matching]]
[F1] [[texp-aqft-finite-heavy-scalar-matching]]: in the finite positive Gaussian sector, $\Delta S_W(J)=-\tfrac12J^TK^{-1}J$, with the stated spectral-band truncation bounds.
associated_steps: 1.1 Here $K=5m_0^2$ is positive, $J$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $E^2=m_0^2$, and $E<M$. Thus $K^{-1}J=1/(5m_0)$ and $S_0J=M^{-2}J=1/(4m_0)$. By [F1], $Z_H(J)=e^{1/10}$ and $\Delta S_W=-1/10$, while the order-zero action is $-\tfrac12J^TS_0J=-1/8$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The vector remainder is $|1/(5m_0)-1/(4m_0)|=1/(20m_0)\le1/(16m_0)$, the bound in [F1] for $N=0$. The action remainder is $|-1/10+1/8|=1/40$, while [F1] bounds it by $\tfrac12(m_0^2/(4m_0^2))(m_0^2/(4m_0^2))=1/32$. Both inequalities are exact rational comparisons. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

blocks: [Product torus, smooth structure, period-one basis, and Milnor hypotheses] [[def-standard-product-torus-as-a-compact-lie-group]]

[F6] The standard product torus is a well-pointed compact Lie group of CW type; its circle factors satisfy the hypotheses of the selected Milnor join theorem, and its selected degree-one tangent vectors have period one. [[def-standard-product-torus-as-a-compact-lie-group]]
associated_steps: 1.1 By [F6] and the group isomorphism [F7], the Milnor theorem's well-pointed CW-type hypothesis holds for the circle model used in each factor. The product of the $r$ free contractible circle models is free for the coordinatewise product action: if a tuple is fixed by $t=(t_1,\ldots,t_r)$, freeness in each coordinate gives $t_i=1$ for every $i$. It is contractible because a finite product of contractions is a contraction. The quotient map $E_{S^1}\to E_{S^1}/S^1$ is open, since the saturation of an open set is a union of its group translates. Its finite product is an open surjection whose fibers are exactly the $T$-orbits, hence is a quotient map and induces $BT\cong(BS^1)^r\cong(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty})^r$ by [F1]. The assertion is immediate for the empty product $r=0$. [given, F1, F6, F7, construct]

blocks: [Standard product torus and period-one basis] [[def-standard-product-torus-as-a-compact-lie-group]]

[F18] The fixed product torus is a compact connected abelian Lie group, and each period-one basis vector exponentiates to its coordinate circle subgroup as specified in the local torus definition. [[def-standard-product-torus-as-a-compact-lie-group]]
associated_steps: 1.4 Pullback naturality [F13] shows that $d$ preserves the $T$-fixed forms. For $t\in T$, the left action law and commutativity give $a_t\circ a_{\exp(-s e_i)}=a_{\exp(-s e_i)}\circ a_t$; differentiating at $s=0$ shows $(a_t)_*X_{e_i}=X_{e_i}$. By the pointwise definition [F9], contraction by each $X_{e_i}$ preserves invariant forms, while $u_i$ is fixed by the stipulated trivial action on the polynomial factor. Both terms therefore preserve the diagonal $T$-fixed subspace, so $d_T:C_T(M)\to C_T(M)$ is well-defined. [F2, F3, F9, F13, F18, step 1.2, step 1.3]

2.1 Put $\phi_s=a_{\exp(-s e_i)}$. The local torus definition [F18] identifies $\exp(-s e_i)$ with the coordinate one-parameter subgroup, so the group law gives $\phi_{s+h}=\phi_s\circ\phi_h$. Differentiating at $h=0$ gives $\frac{d}{ds}\phi_s(p)=(d\phi_s)_pX_{e_i}(p)=X_{e_i}(\phi_s(p))$ by step 1.4. Thus $\phi_s$ is the flow of $X_{e_i}$. For an invariant form $\alpha$, $\phi_s^*\alpha=\alpha$ for every $s$; differentiating at zero and using [F10] gives $\mathcal L_{X_{e_i}}\alpha=0$. Substitution in step 1.5 proves $d_T^2\alpha=0$ on $C_T(M)$. [F3, F10, F18, step 1.4, step 1.5]

blocks: [Period-one circle exponential] [[def-standard-product-torus-as-a-compact-lie-group]]
[F7] The period-one tangent generator exponentiates as $s\mapsto[s]$. [[def-standard-product-torus-as-a-compact-lie-group]]
associated_steps: 2.1 Integer translations preserve $dx$, so $-dx$ descends through the standard quotient charts to a global smooth one-form $\eta$ on the circle. The circle translations act transitively, so an invariant smooth function is constant. Every smooth one-form is $f(x)dx$ for a smooth periodic function $f$; invariance under all translations forces $f$ constant. Since higher forms vanish on a one-dimensional manifold, the invariant form algebra is spanned by $1$ and $\eta=-dx$. By [F7], the negative-exponential flow is $[x]\mapsto[x-s]$, hence $X_e=-\partial_x$ and $\iota_{X_e}\eta=1$; also $d\eta=0$. Substitution in [F1] gives $d_TP(u)=0$ and $d_T(P(u)\eta)=-uP(u)$. [F1, F5, F6, F7, given]

blocks: [F1] The preceding local lemma constructs a $T$-invariant metric for the given action. [[lem-qftx-compact-torus-fixed-locus-normal-weights]]
associated_steps: 2.2 Each $t\in T$ is an isometry of $g$, so [F3] and uniqueness of geodesics give $E(t\cdot p,(d t)_p v)=t\cdot E(p,v)$. The norm of the normal vector is preserved, so the disk $D_\epsilon(\nu(S))$ and its image are $T$-invariant, proving the equivariant tubular assertion. [F1, F3, step 2.1]

blocks: [F1] The fixed set $F$ is compact with finitely many components, and the normal representation splits into finitely many nontrivial character bundles with a $T$-invariant complex orientation. [[lem-qftx-compact-torus-fixed-locus-normal-weights]]
associated_steps: 1.1 Fix a component $F_0$. The action on $F_0$ is trivial, so its Borel base is $BT\times F_0$. By [F5], the Borel normal bundle is numerable and oriented; hence its Thom and Euler classes exist. By [F4], identify $H_T^*(F_0;k)$ as the graded ring $A_T(k)\otimes_kH^*(F_0;k)$. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F5]

2.1 Fix $p\in F_0$. Restriction of $e_T(\nu_F)$ along $BT\times\{p\}\hookrightarrow BT\times F_0$ is the Euler class of the associated normal representation bundle over $BT$. By [F1], that representation is a sum of nontrivial complex character lines. The associated bundle is the direct sum of the corresponding $L_\chi$, with the stated multiplicities. Whitney multiplication in [F6] and $e(L_\chi)=c_1(L_\chi)$ give the claimed product. Every factor is a generator of $\mathscr S_T(k)$. [F1, F2, F5, F6, step 1.1]

4.1 There are finitely many components by [F1], so $H_T^*(F;k)$ and its localization split into the finite product of the component rings treated in step 3.1. A finite tuple of units is a unit componentwise. If $F=\varnothing$, its cohomology is the zero ring and its unique element is a unit; if a normal component has rank zero, its product in step 2.1 is $1$. These cases include $r=0$, trivial actions, and empty $M$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

blocks: [F1] The fixed set has an invariant tubular disk neighborhood; each orbit has an equivariant tube $T\times_H D(V)$, and every stabilizer in that tube is contained in its proper orbit stabilizer $H$. [[lem-qftx-compact-torus-fixed-locus-normal-weights]] [[lem-qftx-compact-torus-equivariant-slice-neighborhoods]]

For each $x\in K$, [F1] gives an open invariant orbit tube $V_x$ with all stabilizers contained in $H_x$; compactness gives a finite subcover $V_1,\ldots,V_m$ of $K$. For $F

u_F)\subset K$ is compact: cover the compact base by finitely many relatively compact bundle charts; over each compact chart closure the sphere fiber is compact, and the finitely many resulting compact sets cover $Q$. [A1, F1, F6, given, construct]

4.1 Apply step 3.1 with $W_j=V_j$ and then with $W_j=V_j\cap D_ho(

u_F)\setminus F)$, and their intersection is covered by the open sets $V_j\cap(D_ho(
u_F)\setminus F)\subseteq V_j$; step 3.1 makes this intersection localized-acyclic as well. A final localized Mayer–Vietoris sequence gives $\mathscr S_T(k)^{-1}H_T^*(M\setminus F;k)=0$. If $F=\varnothing$, the finite tube union covers all $M$ and step 3.1 applies directly; if $F=M$, the complement is empty. [F1, F5, F7, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎

blocks: [F1] $F$ is a compact embedded submanifold with an invariant tubular disk, and its normal bundle has a componentwise $T$-invariant complex orientation with only nontrivial weights. [[lem-qftx-compact-torus-fixed-locus-normal-weights]] [[lem-qftx-compact-torus-equivariant-slice-neighborhoods]]
associated_steps:
1.1 For any invariant pair $Z\subseteq Y$, use the relative Borel notation of [F6]. Put $X_T=ET\times_T M$ and $A_T=ET\times_T(M\setminus F)$. The fixed set is closed by [F1], so $M\setminus F$ is invariant and open; its Borel construction is open because the quotient map by the diagonal $T$-action is open. The pair long exact sequence [F5] has segment
$$
H_T^{q-1}(M\setminus F;k)\to H_T^q(M,M\setminus F;k)\to H_T^q(M;k)\to H_T^q(M\setminus F;k).
$$
By [F3], after localization both outside terms vanish in every degree, and the sequence remains exact. Hence the relative-to-absolute map
$$
\mathscr S_T(k)^{-1}H_T^*(M,M\setminus F;k)\longrightarrow\mathscr S_T(k)^{-1}H_T^*(M;k)
$$
is an isomorphism. [F3, F5, given, algebra]

H_T^*(M,M\setminus F;k)\cong H^*(ET	imes_TU,ET	imes_T(U\setminus F);k).

The equivariant tubular diffeomorphism identifies this pair with the Borel open disk bundle pair $(D(

e0$, stays inside the open disk and fixes $\overline D_ho$, including $S_ho$. blocks: [Finite-dimensional fixed loci and normal weights] [[lem-qftx-compact-torus-fixed-locus-normal-weights]]
[F2] The fixed-point and normal-weight conventions are those of the compact torus fixed-locus lemma. [[lem-qftx-compact-torus-fixed-locus-normal-weights]]
associated_steps: 1.1 A point $[z_0:z_1]$ is fixed by all $t\in T$ only if one homogeneous coordinate is zero: if both were nonzero, equality $[z_0:e^{2\pi it}z_1]=[z_0:z_1]$ would force $e^{2\pi it}=1$ for every $t$. Thus the fixed points are $p_+$ and $p_-$. In the local coordinate $w=z_1/z_0$ at $p_+$, the action is $w\mapsto e^{2\pi it}w$. In $v=z_0/z_1$ at $p_-$, it is $v\mapsto e^{-2\pi it}v$. These give the stated weights and character classes $u$ and $-u$, both inverted by $\mathscr S_T(k)$. [F1, F2, algebra]

blocks: [F1] The multiplicative unit circle is a compact metrizable topological group; with basepoint $1$, it has a finite CW structure with $1$ as a zero-cell. [[lem-unit-circle-is-a-compact-metrizable-topological-group]]
associated_steps: 1.1 The identity point is a zero-cell of the finite CW circle, so its inclusion is a relative CW subcomplex inclusion and is a cofibration by [F2]. Together with compact metrizability from [F1], this makes $S^1$ a well-pointed group of CW type in the sense of [F2]. Hence [F3] applies. [F1, F2]

blocks: [[lem-local-holder-cauchy-transform-estimate]]

[F1] The fixed-support Cauchy transform solves $\partial_{\bar w}Tq=q$ and maps compactly supported $C^{m,\alpha}$ data to $C^{m+1,\alpha}$ on every fixed disk with a finite bound. [[lem-local-holder-cauchy-transform-estimate]]
associated_steps: 1.1 First solve one equation with all other coordinates regarded as parameters $p$. Write $z_j=\rho w$ on a disk slightly larger than $|w|\le2$, choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\chi$ supported in $|w|<2$ and equal to one for $|w|\le1$, and put $a_\rho(w,p)=\rho A_j(\rho w,p)$. For fixed $0<\alpha<1$, its $C^\alpha_w$ norm is bounded uniformly on a compact parameter polydisc by $C\rho(M_0+\rho M_1)$, where $M_0,M_1$ bound $A_j$ and its first derivatives. Multiplication is bounded in the matrix Hölder norm by the product rule for increments, and [F1] bounds $K(p)u=T(\chi a_\rho u)$ on $C^\alpha(\overline D_2)$. Choose one positive $\rho$ making $\|K(p)\|<1/4$ for every parameter. By [F3], $g=1-K(p)g$ has a unique fixed point; $\|g-1\|\le\|K\|/(1-\|K\|)<1/3$, so $g$ is invertible everywhere. On $|w|<1$, [F1] gives $\partial_{\bar w}g=-a_\rho g$. [F1, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 The coefficients depend smoothly on parameters as maps into $C^\alpha_w$, since all their parameter derivatives have uniform bounds on compact subsets. The inverse $(1+K(p))^{-1}$ is the uniformly convergent Neumann series; the identity $L(p+h)-L(p)=-L(p+h)(K(p+h)-K(p))L(p)$ for $L=(1+K)^{-1}$ gives its first derivative in operator norm, and induction gives derivatives of every order. Hence $g=L(p)1$ is smoothly parameter-dependent in $C^\alpha_w$. For each such derivative, the fixed-point equation and [F1] gain one $w$ derivative; induction gives all mixed $C^{m,\alpha}_w$ derivatives on the same radius, because only the inverse in the initial $C^\alpha$ space needs smallness. Thus $g$ is jointly smooth. If $A_j$ is holomorphic in an untouched coordinate, $K$ has zero antiholomorphic parameter derivative by [F2], and differentiating the inverse identity gives the same for $g$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Gauge by this $g$ on the smaller disk. The transformed coefficient is $A_i'=g^{-1}(\partial_{\bar z_i}g+A_i g)$, and $A_j'=0$. The square-zero condition in a smooth frame is $\partial_{\bar z_i}A_j-\partial_{\bar z_j}A_i+[A_i,A_j]=0$, and it is preserved by the gauge transformation by direct conjugation of $(D'')^2$. Therefore every remaining $A_i'$ is holomorphic in $z_j$. Kill the next coordinate by steps 1.1–2.1 with a cutoff only in that coordinate. Their holomorphic-parameter assertion preserves $A_j'=0$. Continue through the finitely many coordinates, shrinking the respective coordinate disks as needed. The product of the resulting smooth invertible gauges has all transformed coefficients zero, proving the required local frame. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If $G$ and $H$ are two such frames, $D''G=D''H=0$ gives $\bar\partial(G^{-1}H)=0$. For smooth scalar functions this implies holomorphy: the one-variable Cauchy formula applies with the other variables fixed, and its iterated integral on a product of small circles gives a locally convergent joint power series. Thus the transition matrices are holomorphic, giving [F4]'s bundle structure; any other structure with the same $D''$ has the same class of holomorphic frames, hence agrees. In these frames an intertwining smooth bundle map has matrix $M$ with $\bar\partial M=0$, so is holomorphic by the same calculation, and the converse follows by the Leibniz rule. Rank zero is immediate and the finite gauge induction covers every positive finite rank. [F1, F2, F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

blocks: [F7] [[thm-global-schauder-regularity-for-the-weak-dirichlet-laplacian]]: on a bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ disk, a weak zero-Dirichlet solution of $-\Delta v=f$ with $f\in C^{0,\alpha}$ has a unique representative in $C^{2,\alpha}$.
associated_steps: 3.1 Set $G_R(v)=\kappa+L_Rv-\kappa A_Re^v$ and choose $L_R\ge\kappa\max_{\overline D_R}(A_Re^{\psi_R})$. For $v\le\psi_R$, $G_R'(v)=L_R-\kappa A_Re^v\ge0$, so the iteration map $T_R=(-\Delta+L_R)^{-1}G_R$ is order preserving. The subsolution inequality from step 2.1 gives $v_0\le T_Rv_0$ and the supersolution inequality from step 1.2 gives $T_R\psi_R\le\psi_R$, by positivity of the resolver in step 1.3. Thus $v_0\le v_1\le\cdots\le\psi_R$; every iterate after $v_0$ has zero Dirichlet trace. Each has a smooth representative: starting from smooth $v_0$ and $A_R$, rewrite its shifted resolvent equation as a Laplace equation, use boundedness and [F5] for $W^{2,p}$, then [F6]–[F7] and local bootstrapping; this also identifies continuous representatives up to the boundary. These representatives realize the order pointwise. [F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra]

[F2] [[thm-sobolev-compactness-and-elliptic-estimates-give-fredholm-hodge-decomposition]] and [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]] give the weak regularity and shifted inverse for a formally symmetric scalar-symbol Laplace-type operator on the compact product.
associated_steps: 1.2 Chirality anticommutes with $D_4$ and is parallel, so $D_5^2=D_4^2-\partial_t^2$. It has scalar positive principal symbol and smooth coefficients. Formal symmetry follows from unitary connection compatibility and periodic integration by parts. The same shifted-resolvent argument applies to $D_4$ and $D_5$ on a general compact background: each square has scalar positive principal symbol, and [F2] gives the inverse of its positive shift from $L^2$ to $H^2$; multiplying by $D_j\mp i$ gives surjectivity of $D_j\pm i$ and the $H^1$ selfadjoint domain exactly as in [F1]. An $L^2$ weak chiral cokernel vector also has square zero distributionally; testing against smooth sections and using their $H^2$ density puts it in the adjoint domain of the selfadjoint square, hence in $H^2$, and [F2] then makes it smooth. This justifies identifying the cokernel with the negative-chirality kernel. Weak kernels are smooth by the same argument. For a zero mode $\psi$, integration by parts gives $0=\|D_5\psi\|^2=\|D_4\psi\|^2+\|\partial_t\psi\|^2$. Thus $\psi$ is independent of $t$ and lies in $\ker D_4$; conversely every such spinor gives a periodic product zero mode. In general its complex dimension is $n_++n_-$, identifying the smooth negative-chirality kernel with the cokernel by the formal $L^2$ adjoint. For the concrete round twist this dimension is $1$ by [F1]. This avoids any unproved general spectral-flow identity. [given, A1, F1, F2, algebra]

blocks: [F4] Every bounded sequence in $H^{k+1}$ of sections on the compact manifold has a subsequence converging in $H^k$. [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]], assertion 1.
associated_steps: 2.2 By [F4], a subsequence converges strongly in $H^k$ to a section $u$. The $H^k\hookrightarrow C^0$ embedding preserves the pointwise $SU(N)$ equations and the bundle transition law, so $u$ is a group-bundle section. In the gauge equation, $A_j\to A$, $B_j\to B$, and $u_j\to u$ in $H^k$; because $H^k$ is an algebra, $u_jB_j-A_ju_j\to uB-Au$ in $H^k$. Thus $du_j$ converges in $H^k$ and the local coefficients converge in $H^{k+1}$. The limit satisfies $du=uB-Au$, equivalently $B=A^u$, and $u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.2]

blocks: [F3] For a smooth connection $A_0$, $\Delta_{A_0}$ is a smooth-coefficient, formally symmetric, nonnegative Laplace-type operator; the compact Hodge theorem gives a finite-dimensional smooth kernel, closed range, and the decomposition $H^r=\ker\Delta_{A_0}\oplus\Delta_{A_0}(H^{r+2})$ for every integer $r\ge0$. [[thm-sobolev-compactness-and-elliptic-estimates-give-fredholm-hodge-decomposition]], [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]]

[F4] The compact Sobolev inclusions $H^{s+1}\hookrightarrow H^s$ hold for all integer $s\ge0$, and the smooth reference operator has the elliptic estimate $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}\le C(\|\Delta_{A_0}\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}+\|\xi\|_{L^2})$. [[thm-sobolev-compactness-and-elliptic-estimates-give-fredholm-hodge-decomposition]], [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]]
associated_steps:
1.1 Fix the smooth reference connection $A_0$ from the configuration data and set $h=A-A_0\in H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$. In a local orthonormal frame, $d_A=d_{A_0}+[h,\cdot]$ on zero-forms and $d_A^*=d_{A_0}^*-\iota_h$ on one-forms, where $\iota_h(a)=g^{ij}[h_i,a_j]$. Therefore $K_A:=\Delta_A-\Delta_{A_0}$ is a finite sum of terms of the forms $(
abla_{A_0}h)\xi$, $h
abla_{A_0}\xi$, and $h^2\xi$. These terms define a bounded map $H^{k+1}	o H^{k-1}$. They are compact: $(
abla_{A_0}h)\xi$ factors through the compact inclusion $H^{k+1}\hookrightarrow H^{k-1}$ followed by multiplication in the algebra $H^{k-1}$; $h
abla_{A_0}\xi$ and $h^2\xi$ first map boundedly into $H^k$ and then use the compact inclusion $H^k\hookrightarrow H^{k-1}$. Here $k-1>d/2$, so the needed multiplication bounds follow from [F8]. [given, A1, F4, F8, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F3] with $r=k-1\ge0$ to $\Delta_{A_0}:H^{k+1}\to H^{k-1}$. Its kernel is finite dimensional, and the Hodge theorem gives the topological direct decomposition $H^{k-1}=\ker\Delta_{A_0}\oplus\Delta_{A_0}(H^{k+1})$. Thus its range is closed with codimension equal to the kernel dimension, so $\Delta_{A_0}$ is Fredholm of index zero. By [F6] and the compactness of $K_A$ from step 1.1, $\Delta_A=\Delta_{A_0}+K_A$ is Fredholm of index zero. [F3, F6, step 1.1]

2.2 The smooth reference estimate [F4] and $\Delta_{A_0}=\Delta_A-K_A$ give $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}\le C(\|\Delta_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}+\|K_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}+\|\xi\|_{L^2})$. The three terms in $K_A$ from step 1.1 satisfy $\|K_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}\le C_A\|\xi\|_{H^k}$. The Sobolev interpolation estimate $\|\xi\|_{H^k}\le\varepsilon\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}+C_\varepsilon\|\xi\|_{L^2}$ follows by finite-atlas localization and the estimate in [F5]. Choose $\varepsilon$ so that the resulting $H^{k+1}$ term is absorbed into the left side. This yields $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}\le C_A'(\|\Delta_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}+\|\xi\|_{L^2})$. [F4, F5, F8, step 1.1, algebra]

4.2 If no constant bounded $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}$ by $\|\Delta_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}$, choose $\|\xi_j\|_{H^{k+1}}=1$ with $\Delta_A\xi_j\to0$. By [F4], a subsequence converges in $L^2$; applying the estimate of step 2.2 to differences shows it is Cauchy in $H^{k+1}$. Its limit has $H^{k+1}$ norm one and lies in $\ker\Delta_A$, contradicting step 3.1. Thus $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}\le C_A''\|\Delta_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}$. Together with bijectivity this proves the inverse $G_A$ is bounded. [F4, step 3.1, step 2.2]

blocks: [F6] For a smooth-coefficient elliptic operator on a compact manifold, distributional solutions gain two Sobolev derivatives when the right-hand side gains the corresponding Sobolev order, with the stated elliptic estimate. [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]]
associated_steps: 5.2 For the smooth-space clause, fix now a smooth irreducible center $A\in\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and use the Banach slice and trivialization established in step 4.1. Put $U_A=\Phi_A(S_{A,\varepsilon}\times\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1})$ and $V_A=\pi_k(S_{A,\varepsilon})$. Since $U_A$ is open in $\mathcal A_k^*$, $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open in the stated $C^\infty$ topology; set $S_A^\infty=S_{A,\varepsilon}\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and $V_A^\infty=\pi_\infty(S_A^\infty)$. For a smooth $B\in U_A$, its unique reduced gauge class from step 4.1 has a representative $u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}$. It satisfies $d_A^*(B^{u^{-1}}-A)=0$. Locally in a bundle frame, write $C_j=uB_j u^{-1}-(\partial_j u)u^{-1}-A_j$. Substitution in $d_A^*C=0$, use of $\partial_i(u^{-1})=-u^{-1}(\partial_i u)u^{-1}$, and multiplication on the right by $u$ isolate the equation $g^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j u=R(A,B,g;u,u^{-1},du)$ on each chart. Every term in $R$ is a finite product of smooth coefficients (including first derivatives of $A,B$) and factors among $u,u^{-1},du$; hence the principal operator is the scalar smooth Laplacian on each matrix entry. If $u\in H^{r+1}$ for $r\ge k$, then this right-hand side lies in $H^r$ by [F7] and the smooth coefficient bounds. Elliptic regularity [F6] gives $u\in H^{r+2}$. Iteration proves $u$ smooth; changing its representative by an element of the finite center preserves smoothness. Thus every smooth point of the Banach saturation has a smooth trivialization representative, and $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*=\pi_\infty^{-1}(V_A^\infty)$. [F1, F2, F6, F7, step 4.1]

6.1 Suppose smooth $B_j\to B$ in $C^\infty$ within $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$. The Banach trivialization from step 4.1 gives convergence of their slice representatives in $H^k$ and of their reduced gauge classes in $H^{k+1}$. In a quotient chart around the limiting class from step 1.1, choose lifts $u_j,u$ that converge in $H^{k+1}$; this is possible because the finite center acts by disjoint translates. The equation in step 5.2 and elliptic estimates [F6] bootstrap convergence: if $u_j\to u$ in $H^{r+1}$, then the assumed $C^\infty$ convergence gives $B_j\to B$ in $H^{r+1}$, and [F7] makes the right-hand sides converge in $H^r$. Apply the elliptic estimate to $u_j-u$, using also their already known $H^{k+1}$ convergence for the $L^2$ term, to get $u_j\to u$ in $H^{r+2}$. Induction gives convergence in every Sobolev order, which on compact $M$ is the $C^\infty$ section topology. The slice representatives converge in $C^\infty$ by their action formula. Conversely the forward action is continuous in the $C^\infty$ topology by multiplication and differentiation of smooth sections. The saturation $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open, and $V_A^\infty$ is open in the quotient because the quotient map is open: the saturation of any open set is a union of its open gauge translates. The restricted map $S_A^\infty\times\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty\to\pi_\infty^{-1}(V_A^\infty)$ is therefore a homeomorphism for the actual quotient topology, and it is equivariant. This proves the smooth-space topological principal bundle claim. [F1, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 5.2] ∎

blocks: [F2] On a bounded extension domain, $W^{k,2}$ is a Banach algebra when $2k>d$, and the higher-order embedding gives $H^k\hookrightarrow C^1$ when $k>d/2+1$. The same estimates apply componentwise to finitely many localized bundle coefficients. [[cor-sobolev-algebra-above-the-critical-index]], [[thm-higher-order-sobolev-embedding]]
associated_steps: 2.1 Localize by the fixed finite partition and extend each compactly supported coefficient by zero into a bounded Euclidean ball. For $p=2$, $2k>d$; [F2] makes each localized $H^k$ coefficient a Banach algebra and gives its $C^1$ representative when $k>d/2+1$. The finite sum of these estimates proves the same algebra and embedding bounds for sections, matrix-valued functions, and forms in the chosen bundle atlas. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 The finite-dimensional matrix exponential is smooth, has derivative the identity at zero on $\mathfrak{su}(N)$, and maps $\mathfrak{su}(N)$ into $SU(N)$. In the Banach algebra from step 2.1 its power series and every termwise derivative converge in $H^{k+1}$ on a sufficiently small ball, since the algebra norm is submultiplicative after an equivalent rescaling. The matrix logarithm series converges on a neighborhood of the identity; for a unitary matrix sufficiently close to identity its logarithm is anti-Hermitian, and its trace is zero because the determinant is one and the sum of the small eigenvalue angles lies in $2\pi\mathbb Z$. Hence pointwise $\exp$ and $\log$ give inverse smooth maps between neighborhoods of zero in $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ and the identity in $\mathcal G_{k+1}$. The inverse-function theorem [F3] also supplies these local Banach charts. Their translated charts cover the group; changes of chart are smooth because the transition functions of $\operatorname{Ad}P$ act by smooth conjugation and the multiplication is a bounded bilinear Sobolev map. The pointwise product and inverse therefore close on $\mathcal G_{k+1}$ and are smooth, giving the asserted Hilbert Lie group. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1]

blocks: [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains|Divergence theorem on bounded C1 domains]]

[F4] For a bounded $C^1$ domain and a $C^1$ vector field on its closure, the integral of the divergence equals the outward boundary flux; this theorem assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]]
associated_steps: 2.1 On each closed ball $B_R$, $J$ is $C^1$, so [F4] and step 1.1 give $\int_{B_R}\sum_i\kappa(D_i\Phi,B_i)\,d^3x=\int_{S_R^2}\kappa(\Phi,B_i)\hat x_i\,dS$. Positive definiteness in [F2] gives $2|\kappa(D_i\Phi,B_i)|\le\kappa(D_i\Phi,D_i\Phi)+\kappa(B_i,B_i)$, so finite energy makes the cross term integrable. Taking $R\to\infty$ and using the declared surface limit yields $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_i\kappa(B_i,D_i\Phi)\,d^3x=m$. [A1, F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

blocks: [F3] A domain is Hartogs pseudoconvex when $-\log\delta_\Omega$ is plurisubharmonic, where $\delta_\Omega$ is the equal-radius polydisc boundary function; the whole-space convention makes $\mathbb C$ Hartogs pseudoconvex. On such domains the scalar holomorphic structure sheaf has zero positive-degree sheaf cohomology ([[def-plurisubharmonic-exhaustion-and-hartogs-pseudoconvexity]], [[def-polydisc-boundary-radius]], [[lem-qftx-gaga-scalar-pseudoconvex-acyclicity]]).

[A1] Full AC is the set-choice postulate and is included in the local Oka and scalar-acyclicity inputs ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-qftx-gaga-analytic-oka-coherence]], [[lem-qftx-gaga-scalar-pseudoconvex-acyclicity]]).
associated_steps: 1.1 By [F7], $\mathcal O(-2)$ is coherent, and its displayed frames trivialize it on $U_0$ and $U_1$. The domain $U_0\cong\mathbb C$ is Hartogs pseudoconvex by the whole-space convention. On $U_0\cap U_1\cong\mathbb C^*$, the equal-radius disk boundary function is $\delta(z)=|z|$, so $-\log\delta(z)=-\log|z|$ is harmonic and has zero Levi form; it is plurisubharmonic by [F4], hence the overlap is Hartogs pseudoconvex. The same argument applies to $U_1\cong\mathbb C$. By [F3], $\mathcal O$ and thus $\mathcal O(-2)$ are acyclic on every nonempty member and overlap. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F7, given, construct]

blocks: [F1] Fourier transformation preserves Schwartz space continuously, with its differentiation and polynomial-multiplication identities; Fourier inversion holds there. Rescaling frequency from the suppliers' $2\pi$ convention gives the convention in the Statement. [[thm-fourier-transform-maps-schwartz-space-continuously-to-itself]], [[thm-fourier-inversion-on-schwartz-space]]
associated_steps: 1.1 Work in one precompact bundle chart and write $p(y,\xi)=\sum A^{ij}(y)\xi_i\xi_j$. The matrices need not commute. For a parameter derivative, the matrix exponential satisfies $\partial e^{-p}=-\int_0^1e^{-(1-s)p}(\partial p)e^{-sp}\,ds$, obtained by differentiating the matrix ODE defining the exponential. Iterating this identity and differentiating in $\xi$ expresses every derivative in $y,\xi$ as finitely many simplex integrals of products of polynomial derivatives of $p$ and exponential factors whose time lengths sum to one. Since $p\ge c'|\xi|^2I$ uniformly on the chart closure, the product norm is at most a polynomial in $|\xi|$ times $e^{-c'|\xi|^2}$. Thus $e^{-p(y,\cdot)}$ is a uniformly bounded smooth Schwartz family. By [F1] its inverse transform $k_y(w)$ has all uniformly bounded Schwartz seminorms, and $\int k_y(w)\,dw=e^{-p(y,0)}=I$. This uses Fourier inversion on Schwartz functions, not an exchange of an undamped double Fourier integral. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Let $\kappa_i$ be finitely many charts with smooth unitary frames, and let $\phi_i$ be a partition subordinate to compact subsets of those charts. Choose smooth cutoffs $\chi_i(y,z)$ supported where both points lie in chart $i$, equal to one near $y=z$ whenever $z\in\operatorname{supp}\phi_i$. Write volume as $w_i(z)\,d\kappa_i(z)$. Define $Z_t(y,z)$ in these frames by the finite sum of $\phi_i(z)\chi_i(y,z)w_i(z)^{-1}t^{-n/2}k_{i,z}((\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z))/\sqrt t)$, interpreting each summand as a bundle map. In each summand the principal coefficients are frozen at the source $z$. Step 1.1, local equivalence of chart distance and $d$, and cutoff support give $\|Z_t(y,z)\|\le C_LH_{t,L}(y,z)$, where $H_{t,L}=t^{-n/2}(1+d(y,z)/\sqrt t)^{-L}$. Moreover $Z_tf\to f$ in $L^2$ for smooth $f$: put $\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z)=\sqrt t\,v$, use the uniform integrable Schwartz bound, and use $\sum_i\phi_i=1$ and $\int k_{i,y}=I$. For $R_t=(\partial_t+P_y)Z_t$, the frozen principal part cancels $\partial_t$. The remaining principal term contains $A(y)-A(z)=O(d(y,z))$ and two derivatives of the frozen kernel; lower terms contain at most one derivative. The bound $d(y,z)t^{-1}H_{t,L+1}\le t^{-1/2}H_{t,L}$ therefore gives $\|R_t(y,z)\|\le C_Lt^{-1/2}H_{t,L}(y,z)$. Derivatives of cutoffs are supported away from the diagonal and obey the same bound by choosing additional Schwartz decay. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 Fix $x$ and put $y=\exp_x(\sqrt t\,a)$, $z=\exp_x(\sqrt t\,b)$. In a chart, Taylor expansion gives $(\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z))/\sqrt t\to d\kappa_i|_x(a-b)$, the frozen symbol tends to $p_i(x,\xi)$, and all frame maps, partition weights and density factors tend to their values at $x$. Linear change of cotangent variables in the absolutely convergent Fourier integral transforms each limiting chart expression into $\phi_i(x)k_x(a-b)$: the coordinate Jacobian cancels $w_i(x)$ because normal-coordinate volume density at $x$ is one. Summing gives $k_x(a-b)$. All convergences are uniform on bounded $a,b$ by step 1.1. By step 4.1, $t^{n/2}\|K_t-Z_t\|\le C\sqrt t$, so it has zero limit. This proves the rescaled limit and all assertions for $n>0$. If $M$ is empty the claims are vacuous; for $n=0$, compact $M$ is finite and differential operators act separately on its fibers, so ordinary matrix exponentiation gives exactly the asserted finite-dimensional limit. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

blocks: [[post-qftx-rigid-supersymmetric-background|Adopted S4 model and gauge-fixed Q-square]]

[A1] [[post-qftx-rigid-supersymmetric-background]]: the adopted model is the source-qualified Euclidean massless $\mathcal N=4$ $SU(2)$ theory on round $S^4_r$; its total gauge-fixed transformation is $Q=s+\delta$ and its square on fields and ghosts is $\delta_{\rm gauge}(a_0)+\delta_{U(1)}(\omega)$. The source's functional measure and S4 noncommutative regulator extension remain formal assumptions.
associated_steps: 1.1 By [A1], the physical input fixes the S4 background and the total gauge-fixed Q-square but does not assert nilpotency. The background definition [F1] says a formal measure is not a constructed measure. Under [A2], $Q_\rho$ is the regulator-preserving realization of that transformation, and the required Q-squared condition is imposed on $V_\rho E_{\rho,t}$. [given, A1, A2, F1]

blocks: [F1] [[def-abbv-equivariant-integration-conventions]]: $H_T^*(X;\mathbb R)=H^*(ET\times_T X;\mathbb R)$, equivariant integration is the degree-shifting pushforward of the Borel fibration, and the Euler class is the zero-section pullback of a Thom class normalized to integrate to $1$ on each oriented fiber.
associated_steps: 1.1 Average any Riemannian metric on $M$ over normalized Haar measure on $T$ to obtain a $T$-invariant metric. The normal exponential map is $T$-equivariant; its derivative is invertible along the zero section, so the inverse function theorem and compactness of $N$ give a $T$-invariant tubular neighborhood identified with $\nu$. Since $T$ fixes $N$ pointwise, $ET\times_T N\cong BT\times N$, and the Borel normal bundle $ET\times_T\nu$ is an oriented rank-$c$ vector bundle over the space $BT\times N$ of CW type. [given, A2, F1, construct]

3.1 Use the tubular-neighborhood identification and excision to transfer $\tau_\nu$ to $H_T^c(M,M\setminus N;\mathbb R)$. For each $\beta\in H_T^*(N;\mathbb R)$, define $i_*^T(\beta)$ as the image of the cup product of this relative Thom class with the pullback of $\beta$ under the relative-to-absolute map $H_T^*(M,M\setminus N;\mathbb R)\to H_T^*(M;\mathbb R)$. This canonical composite is the Gysin map and is defined for every $\beta$ by the Thom isomorphism. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Pull the relative class in step 3.1 back along the zero section. By the definition of $e_T(
u)$ in [F1], the pulled-back Thom class is $e_T(
u)$, and pullback respects cup products. Hence $i^*i_*^T( eta)=e_T(
u)\smile eta$. [given, A1, F1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.3 In the tubular-neighborhood representative from step 3.1, integrate first along each oriented normal disk fiber. The Thom class integrates to $1$ by its fiber normalization, so this fiber integration returns $\beta$ on $N$; the orientation convention in the Statement makes the resulting base orientation the one used by $\int_N$. [given, A1, F1, step 3.1, algebra]

blocks: [F1] [[def-abbv-equivariant-integration-conventions]]: $\mathcal R=H^*(BT;\mathbb R)$, $S$ is generated by the nonzero character classes $u_\chi$, and $e_T(E)$ is the zero-section pullback of a fiber-normalized Borel Thom class.
associated_steps: 4.1 The torus acts trivially on $F_j$, hence $ET\times_TF_j\cong BT\times F_j$ and the Künneth isomorphism over $\mathbb R$ gives $H_T^*(F_j;\mathbb R)=H^*(F_j;\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal R$. Restrict $e_T(\nu_j)$ to any point of $F_j$. The normal representation is the direct sum of the complex character lines in step 3.1; the Euler class of a direct sum is the product because the product of the normalized Thom classes restricts to the positive generator on each direct-sum fiber and hence is its normalized Thom class. By [F1] each line has Euler class $u_{\chi_{j,a}}$, and the orientation comparison gives $f_j=\epsilon_j\prod_a u_{\chi_{j,a}}$ as the degree-zero-in-$H^*(F_j)$ component. Every factor is nonzero and belongs to $S$, so $f_j$ is a unit in $S^{-1}\mathcal R$. [given, A1, F1, F2, step 3.1, algebra]

blocks: [F1] [[def-abbv-equivariant-integration-conventions]]: a character of weight $m$ has equivariant Euler class $m u$ in real Borel cohomology; equivariant integration uses the complex orientation.
associated_steps: 1.1 A point $[z_0:z_1]$ is fixed by every $\lambda$ precisely when it lies on one coordinate axis, so the fixed set is $\{p_0,p_\infty\}$. In the coordinate $w=z_1/z_0$ near $p_0$, the action is $w\mapsto\lambda w$, giving tangent weight $+1$; in $v=z_0/z_1$ near $p_\infty$, it is $v\mapsto\lambda^{-1}v$, giving weight $-1$. The complex orientations agree with $M$, so the Euler denominators are $u$ and $-u$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 The tautological fiber at $p_0$ is the trivial coordinate line, and at $p_\infty$ it is the weight-$+1$ coordinate line. Dualizing gives the fixed-fiber weights $0$ and $-1$ for $\mathcal O(1)$, hence $x|_{p_0}=0$ and $x|_{p_\infty}=-u$. [given, F1, algebra]

3.1 The linear functional $\ell(z_0,z_1)=z_0$ defines a section of $\mathcal O(1)$ that vanishes only at $p_\infty$. In the local coordinate $v=z_0/z_1$ and the dual tautological frame there, its coefficient is $v$, so its unique zero is transverse with positive local degree $+1$. Pulling the normalized Thom class back by a transverse section counts its isolated zeros with these local degrees: excision reduces the pairing to the degree of the section on the boundary of a small disk around each zero. Hence the ordinary Euler number is $1$. Restricting the Borel pushforward to the basepoint of connected $BT$ gives this ordinary Euler number, and $H^0(BT;\mathbb R)=\mathbb R$; therefore $\int_{\mathbb{CP}^1}x=1$, independently confirming the localized sum. [given, A1, F1, step 1.2] ∎

blocks: [F1] [[def-abbv-equivariant-integration-conventions]]: equivariant integration is real Borel fiber integration, a character of weight $m$ has Euler class $m u$, and the product orientation fixes the component-integration signs.
associated_steps: 1.1 The first-factor action fixes exactly $p_0=[1:0]$ and $p_\infty=[0:1]$, while it fixes every point of the second factor. Thus $M^T=F_0\sqcup F_\infty$, with each component a copy of $\mathbb{CP}^1$. The normal bundle is the tangent line of the first factor at its fixed point; in the coordinates $z_1/z_0$ and $z_0/z_1$ its weights are $+1$ on $F_0$ and $-1$ on $F_\infty$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 The normal complex line is the first factor and the fixed-component tangent space is the second. Moving the real two-dimensional first-factor orientation past the real two-dimensional second-factor orientation has sign $(-1)^{2\cdot2}=+1$, so the induced component orientations agree with the product orientations. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The dual tautological fiber at $p_0$ has weight $0$ and at $p_\infty$ has weight $-1$, so the first-factor class restricts to $0$ and $-u$. Thus the contribution from $F_0$ is $0/u=0$; on $F_\infty$, the restricted class is $(-u)\eta$ and the normal Euler class is $-u$, leaving $\eta$, whose integral is $1$. The fixed-component sum is therefore $1$. [given, A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Product fiber integration factors over the two compact oriented factors. On the first $\mathbb{CP}^1$, the section of $\mathcal O(1)$ induced by $\ell(z_0,z_1)=z_0$ has one positive transverse zero at $p_\infty$, so its Euler integral is $1$ by the normalized Thom-class zero count; the second-factor integral of $\eta$ is $1$ by definition. Hence $\int_M\alpha=1\cdot1=1$, agreeing with step 3.1. [given, A1, F1, step 3.1] ∎

blocks: [[thm-atiyah-bott-berline-vergne-integration-formula|Compact ABBV formula]]

[F2] [[thm-atiyah-bott-berline-vergne-integration-formula]]: the current statement is the real Borel fixed-component and isolated-fixed-point formula for compact oriented smooth $T$-manifolds without boundary. It does not cover noncompact instanton spaces.

associated_steps: 2.1 Smoothness of the needed primitive does not require a theorem about varying complex structures. These identify the vertical problem exactly with the fixed $SU(2)$-invariant Hermitian $\mathcal O(-2)$ problem on $\mathbb CP^1$, componentwise in $E_x$. Set $B=\bar\partial^*G$ on vertical degree one. By [F3], $\bar\partial B=I-\Pi$, and by [F2] its degree-zero kernel is zero. The estimates [F4] and the first-order nature of $\bar\partial^*$ give $B:H^m\to H^{m+1}$ bounded for each $m$. For jointly smooth $f(x,t)$, base difference quotients converge in every fibre $H^m$ uniformly on compact base sets, by the Taylor formula and compactness of the fibre. Applying the fixed bounded $B$ shows $\partial_x^\beta(Bf)=B(\partial_x^\beta f)$ at every order in every $H^{m+1}$. Sobolev embedding on the fixed two-dimensional compact fibre, with arbitrarily large $m$, gives joint smoothness in $(x,t)$. For the horizontal coefficient problem, choose also a smooth unit quaternionic frame of $Q_x^\perp$. Together the two quaternionic frames give a smooth $Sp(2)$ transformation from a fixed pair of planes to $(Q_x,Q_x^\perp)$. Its complex-linear action on $\mathbb CP^3$ is holomorphic and preserves the Fubini–Study and tautological metrics. It therefore transports the horizontal quotient, its vertical Bott operator and its induced metric to the fixed $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}$ problem identified below. That inverse is likewise one fixed bounded operator componentwise, so the same derivative argument applies. Thus no moving-cokernel inverse or unproved parametric Green assertion is used. [A2, F2, F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

blocks: [F5] The fixed compact fibre Green inverse is bounded $H^m\to H^{m+2}$ for every integer $m\ge0$. [[thm-sobolev-compactness-and-elliptic-estimates-give-fredholm-hodge-decomposition]]
associated_steps: 1.1 For the global metric splitting, the mixed component of $\bar\partial(s\sigma)$ is a vertical degree-one form with coefficient $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}\otimes E_x$. On a fibre it has a unique vertical primitive by [F4]. The fixed-fibre $B=\bar\partial^*G$ construction and smooth-parameter difference-quotient argument in [F2], with the estimates [F5], make that primitive smooth over the base. The same fibrewise uniqueness makes it agree across frame and chart changes. Denote the horizontal correction by $\phi(s)$; then $\psi(s)=s\sigma+\phi(s)$ has zero mixed differential. If $s$ is the image of a closed representative $\alpha$, [F2]'s decomposition and closedness say that its horizontal remainder solves this same mixed equation. The difference is fibrewise holomorphic in $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}\otimes E_x$, hence zero by [F4]. Thus $\psi(s)=\alpha-\bar\partial_F\gamma$ is closed for a class image. The differential can still have a horizontal degree-two component for arbitrary $s$; the curvature component of the metric splitting is retained. [A1, F2, F4, F5, given, construct, algebra]

associated_steps: 5.1 By [F3] and step 4.1, $4\pi v=m=4\pi v\nu$, so $\nu=1$ because $v>0$. Then $T=4\pi v/g^2>0$. Steps 2.1 and 3.1 give $B_i=D_i\Phi$, so [F4] gives $E=T=4\pi v/g^2$. This verifies a classical unit-flux first-order solution and its saturation without asserting a quantum state. [A1, F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

[F5] [[thm-l-two-kernels-give-hilbert-schmidt-operators]]: under full AC and sigma-finite factor measures, a square-integrable kernel defines a bounded operator between the complex $L^2$ spaces with operator norm at most the kernel $L^2$ norm; those $L^2$ spaces have the required Hilbert structure.
associated_steps: 3.2 The slice measures are finite and hence sigma-finite. Under full AC [A1], apply [F5] to the square-integrable kernel $K$ from step 2.2 to obtain a well-defined bounded integral operator $T$ on the complex slice $L^2$ spaces, with $\|T\|\leq\|K\|_2\leq1$. [given, A1, F3, F5, step 2.2]

4.1 Each spatial-link transformation is a left and right translation, so it preserves its Haar factor by [F1]; the rectangle formula and uniqueness in [F6] then show the product slice measure $d\mu_s$ is preserved. Under independent gauge transformations $h,h'$ of the incoming and outgoing slices, change temporal-link variables by $\eta_x\mapsto h_x\eta_x(h'_x)^{-1}$. Each such coordinate map also preserves Haar factors by [F1], and thus preserves $d\mu_V$ by [F6]. Substitution in $Q_{x,i}=\eta_xU'_{x,i}\eta_{x+\hat i}^{-1}U_{x,i}^{-1}$ cancels the neighboring $h'$ matrices and gives $Q_{x,i}\mapsto h_xQ_{x,i}h_x^{-1}$; each spatial plaquette is likewise conjugated at its base vertex. Trace invariance therefore preserves $S_t,S_s$, and the temporal integration gives $K(h'\cdot u',h\cdot u)=K(u',u)$ for every pair $(h',h)$. In particular, setting $h=1$ gives $K(h'\cdot u',u)=K(u',u)$. The integral representation in [F5], applied almost everywhere, then gives $(T\psi)(h'\cdot u')=(T\psi)(u')$ almost everywhere for each fixed $h'$, so $T\psi\in\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$. The constant function has norm one because $d\mu_s$ is a probability and is fixed by every gauge transformation, so it is a nonzero physical vector. [given, A1, F1, F3, F5, F6, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 Each $\mathcal U(h)$ is unitary by measure preservation from step 4.1; the Hilbert structure follows from [F5] under full AC [A1]. Its fixed space is the kernel of the bounded operator $\mathcal U(h)-I$, hence is closed; the intersection over all $h$ is $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$, so $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$ is closed. [given, A1, F5, step 4.1, algebra]

blocks: [L1] Positive matrix-symbol second-order operators with the stated spectral heat data have the locally uniform rescaled tangent kernel, normalized tangent integral $\int k_x(w)\,dw=I$, and, for every $L>n$, the estimate $\|K_t(y,z)\|\le C_Lt^{-n/2}(1+d(y,z)/\sqrt t)^{-L}$. The proof constructs a frozen-coefficient kernel and its convergent Volterra correction; no scalar-principal-symbol assumption is used. [[lem-equivariant-rescaled-heat-kernel-extension]]
associated_steps: 1.2 Put $B_j=\sigma(d_j)(x,\xi)$, with $B_{-1}=B_N=0$. The principal symbol on $E^j$ of $\Delta$ is $p_j=B_j^*B_j+B_{j-1}B_{j-1}^*$. If its quadratic form vanishes on $v$, then $B_jv=0$ and $B_{j-1}^*v=0$; exactness gives $v\in\operatorname{im}B_{j-1}$ and also orthogonality to that image, hence $v=0$. Compactness of the unit cotangent sphere bundle gives $p_j(x,\xi)\ge c|\xi|^2I$ uniformly. Thus [L1] applies to $\Delta$, using exactly the given spectral heat data. Its principal symbol may be matrix-valued. [given, L1, A1, algebra]

2.1 Write $n=\dim M$ and $J_x$ for the normal-coordinate volume density. For $y=\exp_x(\sqrt t\,v)$ in the chosen neighborhood, [L1] and step 1.1 imply that $t^{n/2}J_x(\sqrt t\,v)\sum_j(-1)^j\operatorname{tr}(\rho_g^j K_t^j(g^{-1}y,y))$ tends pointwise to $\sum_j(-1)^j\operatorname{tr}(\rho_g^j|_{E_x^j}\,k_{x,1}^j(dg_x^{-1}v,v))$. Simplicity makes $dg_x^{-1}-I$ invertible. Local distance comparison in the normal chart therefore gives $d(g^{-1}y,y)\ge c_x\sqrt t\,|v|$. Choose $L>n$; bounded density, unitary $\rho_g$ and [L1] bound the extended-by-zero rescaled density by $C(1+c_x|v|)^{-L}$, integrable on $T_xM$. Outside these neighborhoods compactness gives $d(g^{-1}y,y)\ge\delta>0$, so [L1] bounds the full complementary trace integral by $C t^{(L-n)/2}\to0$. By [F2], the heat-supertrace limit is consequently the sum of these tangent integrals. No uniform-integral-bound-to-convergence implication is used. [given, L1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Since $dg_x$ is orthogonal, $|\det(dg_x^{-1}-I)|=|\det(I-dg_x)|$. The change of variables $w=(dg_x^{-1}-I)v$ therefore contributes $|\det_{\mathbb R}(I-dg_x)|^{-1}$. By [L1], the constant-coefficient tangent heat kernel has integral $I_{E_x^\bullet}$. Its graded fiber trace after composition with $\rho_g$ is $\sum_j(-1)^j\operatorname{tr}(\rho_g|_{E_x^j})$. For $n=0$, the tangent integral and determinant are both the empty-dimensional values $1$, so the same expression holds. Summing the finitely many contributions proves the stated limit. [L1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
